title: Retracting one import retracts every import ever made through that account and channel
description:
Found by codex while reviewing the multi-bank feedback; verified in the tree.

`SourceId::declared(owner, account, channel)` (crates/iaam-core/src/ids.rs)
derives the source identity from owner, account and channel — nothing else.
`SubmitOperationsRequest.source_label`, documented as "Source label: manual
input, a specific agent, a specific file", is deserialised and never used: it
appears in dto.rs and in contract tests, and nowhere on any production path.

`correct_import` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/correction.rs) retracts every
effective event whose `provenance.source()` equals the given source.

So two imports of two different months through the same account and the same
channel — the ordinary case — share one `SourceId`. `POST /v1/corrections/imports`
is published as "Retract a whole import, keyed on the source that was declared
for it", and it retracts all of them.

This is a destructive operation keyed more coarsely than its own description
claims, and it shipped in the previous wave. The field that would distinguish
the two imports is already in the request and thrown away.
acceptance_criteria:
- Two imports through one account and channel are two identities, so retracting one leaves the other in force.
- `source_label` either enters the identity or is removed from the request; a field accepted and ignored is worse than one that is absent.
- A test imports twice through one account and channel, retracts the second, and asserts the first is still effective.
close_reason: ImportId keys the retraction; SourceId unchanged so cross-import dedup still works. ImportTarget::Unnamed covers rows recorded before the field existed. 805f957

title: An ambiguous transfer has no way to be recorded as ambiguous, so the caller must guess
description:
Reported by an external agent importing two banks. The second bank's export
marked an operation `direction: INNER` with an amount and nothing else — not
which side of it this account was on, and not which account was the other side.

`OperationKind` (crates/iaam-ingest/src/operation.rs) offers `Deposit`,
`Withdrawal`, and `Transfer { to: AccountId, .. }`. The first two assert a
direction the source did not give; the third demands a destination account the
caller does not know. There is no fourth thing to send. So the importer wrote
`deposit`, one of them turned out to be a withdrawal, and it had to be fixed
afterwards by a replacement correction.

The reporter's own sentence is the point: "система говорит, что нельзя
записывать догадки как факты, но текущий workflow практически вынуждает
клиента делать именно это."

And the mechanism to do it right already exists, unreachable. This is the sixth
instance of the pattern — implemented, tested, called by nothing:

- `iaam_ingest::classification::ClassificationResult::Ambiguous { question }`,
  whose own doc comment reads "Cannot be inferred from data and is not covered
  by a rule. Guessing is forbidden."
- `Question::IsTransferInternal { account, counterparty }` — exactly "is this
  counterparty one of your own accounts?" — plus `IsOutflowAFee` and
  `IsInflowIncome`.
- `Counterparty::OwnAccount(to)` deriving `InternalTransfer` without a question
  when the answer IS known.
- `Verdict::NeedsClassification`, published in the API vocabulary and
  constructed by nothing in production (iaam-1ffb).

`classify` is called from one place in the whole workspace: `recompute_plan`,
in its own module. The ingest path never calls it.

So the API cannot express the question, the ingest path never asks it, and the
verdict that would carry it is unreachable — while the code that answers it
sits complete and tested one crate away.
acceptance_criteria:
- An operation whose direction or counterparty the source did not resolve can be submitted as such, and comes back needing the owner's answer rather than recorded as a movement.
- Nothing is written to the journal for it until the owner answers: the balance does not move on a guess.
- `classify` is reached from the ingest path, so `Question::IsTransferInternal` and its siblings are asked instead of being unreachable.
- The owner's answer is recorded as a durable rule, so the next import of the same counterparty does not ask again.
close_reason: Intake accepts the source's observation; a directionless row returns a typed question and moves nothing until answered. Migration 0019. 25b9961

title: An account that belongs to no contour raises no action, so its operations vanish from every report
description:
Reported by an external agent importing two banks into an empty database, and
the mechanism is worse than the report supposes.

crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs: `contour_completion(contours) = !contours.is_empty()`.
The goal "the owner has a contour" is satisfied by ANY contour existing. So
`CreateFirstContour` fires exactly once, when there are none, and after that
the action queue has nothing at all to say about contour membership.

Consequence, and it is the failure the reporter actually hit: accounts created
later — a second bank — belong to no contour. Their operations import
successfully, every verdict is positive, the journal holds every fact, and the
report the owner is looking at does not include them. Nothing anywhere says so.

This is the single highest-value fix in the multi-bank feedback: it is the
mechanism by which a correct import produces a silently incomplete report.
acceptance_criteria:
- An account outside every contour raises an action naming it, whatever number of contours already exist.
- The action offers adding the account to an existing contour, not only creating a new one.
- A test with two contours and one orphaned account proves it: today the queue is silent.
close_reason: Three-state account scope disposition; the undecided state reopens the goal when an account is created. Migration 0017. 805f957

title: The transfer-partner statement is asked before every import and read by nothing
description:
`resolve_transfer_relationships` is emitted for every account, `RequiredForGoal`, and its doc comment (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:1297) states the reason: it is asked **before** anything is imported so that «the import knows what it is looking at».

The import does not know. `list_account_transfer_statements` has exactly two non-test callers: the action queue that decides whether to keep asking (actions.rs:391) and the route that reads it back (routes.rs:1737). It reaches neither classification nor pairing nor the assessment.

What actually turns a printed counterparty into one of the owner's own accounts is `resolve_counterparty` in the import session, and it matches the counterparty string against **account titles**, lowercased and trimmed (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/import_session.rs:1295). That is the sole path to `Counterparty::OwnAccount` and therefore to a derived internal transfer settled without a question.

So the owner answers one question per account, before he is allowed to feel the import is ready, and the answer changes nothing about what the import concludes.
design:
Two defects, and the second is the load-bearing one.

- The statement must reach `assess`. A row whose counterparty resolves to an account the owner has named as a partner of this one is an internal transfer on the owner's own statement; today only a title collision produces that.
- Title matching has to stop being the identity mechanism. It is case-insensitive string equality against a display name the owner can rename at any time, and `counterparty_matches` already counts duplicates because two accounts can share a title. This is the same defect as iaam-34f3 seen from the classification side: an account has no identity a source can name.

Sequence matters: wiring the statement into `assess` without external identifiers just moves the fragility. Do iaam-34f3 first, then let the statement carry partner identities rather than partner titles.

Until it is wired, iaam-9hkc (asked of outside accounts too) is asking a question that costs the owner and buys nothing.
close_reason:
Resolution now tries three tiers in order and stops at the first that matches anything: iaam's own AccountId, then provider_account_id and aliases compared verbatim (decision 0004 defines the value as opaque, so case-folding would be a claim about its meaning) with the alias interval checked against the row's effective date, then title. Stopping at the first matching tier is what makes identity beat rather than tie. The single-candidate requirement survives, so the ambiguity refusal now holds at every tier.

Title matching stays: every account created before 0004 states no identity, so dropping the tier would silently stop recognising their transfers while buying no correctness — its one failure mode is a collision, which is refused rather than guessed. What identity buys is precedence, which was the actual defect: a rename can no longer re-point a resolution.

The owner's statement may withdraw a resolution. It may not make one, break a tie, or supply a direction. The trap was applying it to the candidate set rather than to the resolution: filter candidates and tie-breaking falls out free — two accounts titled alike, one declared a partner, one candidate survives, the row settles as a derived internal transfer with no question. That conclusion would be assembled from two facts neither of which is about this row, which is the shape transfer_pairing refuses, and its failure mode is a journal fact against the wrong account, unasked. The filter is therefore applied after resolution, and a test pins that a statement does not break a tie. Withdrawal is monotone toward more questions and never toward a new fact.

15 tests, 9 failing pre-fix. Merged; make check exits 0.

title: Two processes opening the store race each other through the migrations
description:
`schema::migrate` reads `PRAGMA user_version` outside any transaction and then opens each migration with a plain (deferred) `BEGIN`. Two processes that open the same file at once — the server starting and a CLI command run immediately after — both read version 0, both decide migration 1 is missing, and the loser fails with `table events already exists`. No `busy_timeout` is set either, so lock contention returns SQLITE_BUSY instead of waiting.

Reported by an external reviewer running an import against a fresh Docker database; reproduced by reading crates/iaam-store/src/schema.rs:67 and crates/iaam-store/src/lib.rs:166.
acceptance_criteria: Two `SqliteStore::open` calls against the same fresh file, from two threads, both succeed and leave user_version = SCHEMA_VERSION.
close_reason: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, user_version re-read inside the transaction, busy_timeout set. Plus one finding beyond the diagnosis: PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL is the one place SQLite reports SQLITE_BUSY without consulting busy_timeout, so the switch retries within the same budget — without that the regression test still failed. Test: two threads opening the same file behind a barrier; failed with 'table events already exists' before, passes after, 30 consecutive runs clean. Committed in 58f9add.

title: Nothing outside the journal can be restored after a destructive act
description:
Raised by the owner 2026-09-03: "снэпшоты наверное нужно делать какие-то, чтобы
восстановить после деструктивных действий, всякое бывает."

The journal itself is already safe by construction and this bead is not about
it. It is append-only; `POST /v1/corrections` and `POST /v1/corrections/imports`
write reversal and replacement facts rather than deleting anything, so a wrong
retraction is itself retractable and the history of both survives.

What has no such property is everything beside the journal, all of it ordinary
mutable rows added over the last three waves:

- account scope exclusions (migration 0017) — the owner's statements about which
  accounts are outside the perimeter;
- account transfer statements and partners (0018) — his answers to the discovery
  questions;
- import sessions, their observations and their open questions (0019) — work in
  progress that is deliberately not in the journal;
- classification rules, contour versions, category rules, the instrument
  directory, broker access.

Losing those loses the owner's answers, not his facts — but the answers are what
stop the questions being asked again, and several of them took him real effort.

Also outside any of this: the database file. Corruption or a lost disk takes the
journal with everything else, and nothing in the repository currently says what
to do about that.

Note the name collision to avoid in the design: `iaam-store` already has
"snapshots", meaning cached projections that are rebuilt from the journal. They
are a performance device and are not a backup. A second meaning under one word
will be read as the first.
acceptance_criteria:
- A named recovery story for the state that is not the journal: what is captured, how often, where it lives, and how a restore is performed.
- The journal's own recoverability is stated too, including that a retraction adds a fact rather than removing one, so an owner reading the guarantee does not confuse the two.
- Restoring is exercised, not asserted: a test or a documented drill that takes a capture and brings an instance back from it.

title: The classification question is not reachable from the action queue
description:
Left deliberately by the worker who built the session foundation (iaam-6qsa),
because the queue's frontier lives in `crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs`, which
another worker owned in the same wave.

An unanswered classification question is durable pre-journal state now, but the
only way to learn of one is the ingest response that raised it. Codex's point
during the design review stands: a question that exists only in a response body
is not durable state as far as the agent is concerned — if the response is lost,
the outstanding work is invisible.

Also left, and smaller: `ExternalFlow` rules carry no direction, so a row whose
direction was answered as an external flow is asked again on the next import.
acceptance_criteria:
- A question raised at intake appears in /v1/actions with its typed answer shapes and an operation that answers it.
- Losing the ingest response loses nothing: the outstanding question is still discoverable.
- The item names its subject account, as the other queue items now do.
close_reason: An open question is an item in /v1/actions with its alternatives and the operation that answers it. 33f8724

title: An account fed only by transfers is never asked for a balance, because activity counts one side
description:
Found by the worker building the two-bank scenario (iaam-tk2j), and verified.

`list_account_activity` (crates/iaam-store/src/events.rs) counts an account's
activity with `LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.account = a.id` — the account the
event is *recorded against*. An `EventKind::CashTransfer` carries `from` and
`to` and is recorded against one of them, so the other side sees no event at
all.

Consequence: an account whose entire content arrived by internal transfer — a
savings account fed from a current one, a deposit opened by moving money across
— has `has_business_fact = false`. The queue therefore never asks it for an
opening or a closing balance, and instead offers `start_account_import`, as
though nothing had ever reached it. It holds money at month end and nobody is
asked to confirm the figure.

The same class of silence as iaam-imhy: a predicate that looks at the wrong
population and is quiet rather than wrong. It bites hardest in the multi-bank
contour these beads are about, where moving money between one's own accounts is
the ordinary case.

The two-bank scenario carries the failing assertion already, as
`an_opening_balance_is_asked_for_an_account_that_only_received_transfers`,
ignored and naming this bead.
acceptance_criteria:
- An account that a `cash_transfer` moved money into counts as having business facts, and the queue asks it for an opening and then a closing balance.
- The account is not offered `start_account_import` as though it were empty.
- Coverage dates for such an account reflect the transfers that touched it.
- A test with a savings account whose entire content arrived by internal transfer proves it: today the queue asks it for nothing.
close_reason: Both endpoints of a transfer counted, via EventKind::flow_endpoints(). Coverage dates widen. 25b9961

title: Reclassification asks its question using the answer it is meant to reconsider
description:
Found by codex while reviewing the multi-bank feedback; verified in the tree.

`subject(event)` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/classification.rs) builds the
classification subject for recomputation as:

    description: None,
    source_kind: Some(event.kind.discriminant().to_owned()),

`RuleMatcher` has three fields: `counterparty_account`, `description_contains`
and `kind`. On this path the second can never match, because the description is
always `None` — although `Provenance::description()` retained it. And the third
matches against the event's own kind — `cash_in`, `cash_out` — not against what
the source called the row, which is what a rule written at intake would name.

So recomputation reconsiders a classification using the output of the previous
classification as its input, and two thirds of the matcher is inert.

Compounds iaam-u7pb: even were the plan not discarded, it would be computed from
a subject that cannot see what the rule was written about.
acceptance_criteria:
- A classification subject rebuilt from an event carries the description provenance retained and the source's own kind, not the event's discriminant.
- A rule written on what the bank called the row matches on recompute, as it does at intake.
- Two of the three matcher fields stop being dead on the recompute path.
close_reason: subject() reads provenance description and source_category; no discriminant fallback. 805f957

title: A report says nothing about which accounts it covered, so an incomplete perimeter reads as a whole answer
description:
Found by codex while reviewing the multi-bank feedback.

`DataQualityStatus` and the report's quality fields concern defects inside the
calculation — missing prices, unproven bases, uncovered positions. They can all
be clean while the wrong accounts were selected, because selection happens
before the fold and nothing afterwards can see it.

That is precisely the failure the reporter hit: every verdict positive, quality
clean, and half the money outside the contour the report was computed over.

Completeness of a calculation and completeness of its population are two
statements, and today the report makes only the first.

Related: iaam-imhy (an account in no contour raises no action), iaam-mp5e (the
composition cannot be read back).
acceptance_criteria:
- Every report names the accounts inside its scope, and the accounts known to the system that are outside it.
- The two are distinguishable: deliberately excluded, and not yet dispositioned.
- A report over a perimeter that omits accounts the owner has not ruled on says so, rather than reading as an answer about all the owner's money.
close_reason: Every report carries a population block distinguishing placed-elsewhere from undecided; SKILL.md tells the agent to read it first. 805f957

title: An import session: observations accumulate, are assessed, and commit as one plan
description:
Proposed by the owner ("может быть нужен механизм транзакций... открываем,
импортируем, проверяем, фиксируем") and arrived at independently by codex while
reviewing the multi-bank import feedback. Two routes to the same primitive is
the reason to believe it.

NOT a database transaction. An import needs the owner to answer questions
between steps, and that can take hours or days. A transaction held open across
agent turns blocks every other writer, cannot survive a reconnect or a restart,
and this store already serialises all reads and writes behind one mutex
(iaam-qb8). The durable thing must be application state, not a connection.

What the session is for, in order of what it fixes:

- It is where an observation can sit unresolved. Today the only way to submit is
  as a concluded `Deposit`/`Withdrawal`/`Transfer`, so a bank row saying only
  `INNER` must be guessed at intake (iaam-6qsa).
- It is the only place both legs of a cross-bank transfer can be seen before
  either is committed (iaam-3ul2). Matching after the fact means correcting two
  events that were already wrong.
- It makes the preview honest (iaam-k1xa): the assessment is not a second
  implementation of the import, it is what the import is about to do, addressed
  by a revision that commit checks.
- It answers the owner's actual concern — not needing to roll back — by moving
  the decision before the journal rather than after it.

What it does not change: the journal stays append-only and corrections stay.
Some errors are only found months later, and no amount of pre-commit checking
reaches those.

The architectural line this draws is the valuable part: a session is pre-journal
state. Nothing in the journal is provisional, and nothing provisional is in the
journal.
acceptance_criteria:
## Success Criteria

- An import is an addressable thing with a life: opened, fed observations from one or more sources, assessed, questioned, answered, committed or abandoned.
- Nothing enters the journal until commit. The journal keeps its property that everything in it is a fact somebody asserted.
- The assessment is produced by the code that commits, addressed by a revision, and commit refuses a revision that no longer describes what would happen. Preview and commit cannot drift or race.
- Both legs of a cross-bank transfer are visible in one session before either is committed.
- A typed question about an ambiguous row is durable session state, reachable from /v1/actions after the response carrying it is lost.
- Abandoning a session leaves no trace in the journal; committing leaves no trace of the session's uncertainty except what was resolved.
- A correction is still possible afterwards: the session reduces how often retraction is needed, never the ability to retract.
close_reason: All three children landed. The session exists, holds observations before the journal, asks typed questions, assesses by a revision the commit checks, and pairs cross-source transfers. Remaining: iaam-ifo9 (commit is two store calls). 33f8724

title: Reparsing a document makes the agent resend the owner's statement, which it is not supposed to hold
description:
Found by codex while reviewing the multi-bank feedback; verified in the tree.

`POST /v1/documents/{hash}/reparse` takes `ApiBytes(body)` — the whole workbook,
again (crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs `reparse_document`). The path names a
document by hash and then requires the caller to supply the document.

`iaam-store` already has `insert_document` and `load_document`
(crates/iaam-store/src/documents.rs), used by store tests and by nothing else.
`upload_report` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/documents.rs) parses the bytes
and records rows without storing the document.

This contradicts the founding design directly: "ИИ — внешний клиент", the agent
holds none of the owner's data. As it stands, an agent that wants to reparse
must have kept the owner's statement.

Seventh instance of the pattern: implemented, tested, reachable by nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
- A document uploaded once can be reparsed from what the system stored, without the caller resending its bytes.
- `insert_document` and `load_document` are on the upload and reparse paths rather than only in store tests.
- The founding constraint holds: the agent can drive a reparse while holding none of the owner's data.
close_reason: Upload stores the document, reparse reads it by hash; load_document_by_hash added. 28842eb

title: A synthetic two-bank month that the setup order must survive
description:
Proposed by the external agent whose two-bank import produced a silently
incomplete report. It is the regression test the multi-bank beads share:
iaam-imhy, iaam-j9oi, iaam-7xh3, iaam-6qsa, iaam-3ul2, iaam-k1xa.

Invented data only, per CLAUDE.md: nothing trimmed from a real export, no real
institution, account or amount.

Filed as one bead rather than a criterion repeated in six, so that the scenario
is written once and each fix is measured against the same month.
acceptance_criteria:
- A fixture built from nothing real: two institutions, two or three accounts each, one closed deposit, one internal transfer within a bank, one transfer between banks, one INNER row whose direction the source does not give, one expense, one income.
- Exercised in several orders: sources imported in either order, contour drawn before and after import.
- Asserts: no operation leaves the report because of which contour was chosen; a second contour cannot be created by omission; an ambiguous transfer does not become a deposit; the two legs of a cross-bank transfer can be related; the queue asks about structure before import; the report names which accounts it covers; an opening balance is asked for per account; a correction changes the reports and leaves the journal auditable.
close_reason: Synthetic two-bank month; five assertions pass, four ignored naming iaam-6qsa, iaam-3ul2, iaam-7xh3, iaam-8axt. 28842eb

title: An import can be committed before anything says what it will and will not record
description:
Reported by an external agent importing two banks. The CSV importer did report
that some rows fell outside the contour — but only after the contour had been
created and the import had run. The import succeeded, verdicts were positive,
and part of the rows were absent from the report the owner was shown.

Nothing in the tree previews an import. The only preview that exists is
`preview_category_rule` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/categories.rs), for
category rules.

The shape the reporter asked for: accounts_in_source, accounts_known_to_iaam,
accounts_missing, accounts_outside_contour, transfers_unresolved,
cross_bank_matches, operations_that_will_be_recorded,
operations_that_will_be_ignored.

Worth deciding whether a preview is the right primitive at all, or whether it is
a workaround for the queue not having asked about structure first (iaam-7xh3):
a preview is a second implementation of the import unless it is computed by the
import itself.
acceptance_criteria:
- Before committing, a caller can learn what the import will do: which accounts the source names, which of them iaam knows, which are missing, which fall outside the contour, which operations will be recorded and which ignored, and what is unresolved.
- The answer is computed by the same code that performs the import, so the preview cannot describe a different import from the one that runs.
- An import carrying unresolved rows or unknown accounts does not commit unless the owner has said to skip them.
close_reason: plan_session + revision check + submit over the plan's own candidates; commit refuses a stale revision. 33f8724

title: Creating a classification rule computes which events it corrects and discards the answer
description:
crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/classification.rs, `recompute_history`:

    recompute_plan(&events, &subjects, &rules)
        .map(|_| ())

`recompute_plan` returns `Vec<Correction>` — exactly which events a rule change
requires correcting, computed by the module documented as "the sole place that
determines which events require correction". The wrapper drops it on the floor.

So `create_rule` and `retire_rule` load the whole journal, build every subject,
run the plan, and change nothing. An owner who records a classification decision
sees it apply to nothing already imported.

Found while triaging the multi-bank import feedback (iaam-6qsa), where the
durable-rule half of the answer is what stops the same question being asked on
every import.
acceptance_criteria:
- A rule created or retired either corrects the events its plan names, or the response says plainly that it did not and what the plan holds.
- The plan is not computed and thrown away: whatever is computed is either used or not computed.
- Covered by a test that creates a rule matching an existing event and asserts the event's classification afterwards.
close_reason: create_rule and retire_rule return the plan; applying it is POST /v1/corrections. 805f957

title: The action queue has no discovery stage, so a multi-bank setup order is left for the caller to invent
description:
Reported by an external agent importing two banks into an empty database.

`ActionKind` has eleven variants (actions.rs). Two are existential —
`CreateFirstAccount`, `CreateFirstContour` — and the rest are milestones after
facts exist: import, assertions, coverage gaps, discrepancies, residuals.
Nothing asks about the shape of the world before anything is imported.

For one bank that is survivable: the owner does it by hand. For several the
caller has to invent the order, and inventing it wrongly is how the reporter
ended with two contours and a report showing one bank.

The reporter's proposed stage, as named:
discover_institutions, discover_accounts, map_source_accounts,
select_contour_membership, resolve_transfer_relationships.

Depends on the contour model being unambiguous first (iaam-j9oi, iaam-mp5e) —
a discovery stage that hands the caller back into an ambiguous route buys
nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
- Before import, the queue asks for the structure: which institutions, which accounts belong to each, which accounts are inside the contour, which are external, and which accounts are the two sides of an internal transfer.
- The system proposes candidates and never decides membership itself: contour membership is the owner's statement.
- With two banks and an unresolved transfer, the queue's first item is about structure, not about importing.
close_reason: resolve_transfer_relationships: per-account, closed by the owner's statement, reopened by a new account. Migration 0018. 25b9961

title: POST /v1/contours silently creates a new contour when the caller omits its id
description:
routes.rs `create_contour_version`: `ContourId(request.contour.unwrap_or_else(Uuid::new_v4))`.
One route carries two acts — create a contour, add a version to that contour —
and the destructive one is what an omitted field gives you.

Reported by an external agent importing two banks. Having created a contour for
the first bank, it called the route again for the second and received a second
contour holding only the second bank's account. Both contours exist, every
operation is in the journal, and the report for the newer contour shows one bank.

The route is named `create_contour_version` internally and published at
`POST /v1/contours`, which is the shape a reader takes for "create or update
the contour" — and it is neither.

Related: iaam-mp5e (no read route, so a caller cannot even list what exists) and
iaam-imhy (an account in no contour raises no action).

Decide the shape. The reporter proposes splitting it:
POST /v1/contours creates; POST /v1/contours/{id}/versions versions; GET lists.

The action queue demonstrates the dangerous shape and no other. `first_contour_action`
(crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs) builds a request plan whose `missing` list is
`/title` and `/accounts` — never `/contour`. So the one call the queue ever
shows the agent is the one that mints a contour, and there is no action anywhere
for "add this account to the contour you already have".
acceptance_criteria:
- Creating a contour and versioning an existing one are distinguishable acts. An omitted id is not read as 'make me a new one'.
- A caller who means to add an account to the contour it already has cannot get a second contour by omission.
- Whatever shape is chosen, the response says which contour was written and whether it was new.
close_reason: Create refuses a contour id and names the versions route; created flag distinguishes the two acts. 28842eb

title: Every query parameter in the OpenAPI document was published as a path parameter
description:
Reported by an external agent exercising the running instance, which noticed
it on one route: `/v1/journal/events` "works with query params despite OpenAPI
listing in=path". Verified in the tree, where it is far broader — 42
parameters across 12 operations.

`IntoParams` gives a struct's parameters `in: path` whenever the operation has
any path parameter at all, and says nothing about location when it has none.
No struct in this crate declared `parameter_in`, so every filter on every
report, market, reconciliation, document and journal route was published as a
path parameter: `contour`, `from`, `to`, `as_of`, `currency`, `instrument`,
`board`, `session`, `knowledge_as_of`, `account`, `limit`, `after`, and the
rest.

The server was never wrong — all nine structs are extracted with `ApiQuery`
and read the query string. The document was. A client generated from it could
not send a single filter, and the routes it describes are the entire read
surface.

`ClassificationRuleParams` was dead — declared with `IntoParams`, referenced by
no route and by no `params(...)` — so it was removed rather than annotated.
acceptance_criteria:
- A parameter is documented in `path` exactly when the path template names it, and in `query` otherwise.
- The nine `IntoParams` structs read by `ApiQuery` declare `parameter_in = Query`.
- A contract test checks the whole document structurally, so a route added later is covered on the day it is written.
close_reason: Nine IntoParams structs declare parameter_in = Query; ClassificationRuleParams removed as dead. Structural contract guard added and proved by reverting JournalParams. 95531e6

title: The §11 perimeter is implemented in the core and reachable from nothing
description:
`crates/iaam-core/src/perimeter.rs` implements §11 in full: `NegativeCashClassification` with three cases (`TemporarySettlementDeficit`, `UnsupportedMarginLiability`, `UnclassifiedNegativeCash`), `NegativeCashSpan` carrying account, currency, opening date, resolution date and classification, `PerimeterAssessment::blocks_period_reports` — whose doc says tax and financial reports should refuse calculation for that account while the remainder continues — and `exceptions()` producing reconciliation exceptions. It is tested.

`grep -rn 'perimeter::assess'` outside its own module returns **nothing**. `blocks_reports` has exactly one caller, inside `perimeter.rs` itself, plus tests. Nothing runs the assessment: not the balances report, not the returns report, not the action queue.

So a classification the design says must block a period's reports is computed by code no request ever executes, and the report it was meant to gate answers as if the perimeter did not exist.

This is the third instance of one pattern found in a single review session, and the pattern is the finding:

- `event/correction.rs` — reversal and replacement, resolved into the effective set, reachable by no route (iaam-d2wd).
- `Balances::negative_cash()` — computed, consumed only by the returns calculation, absent from the balances report (iaam-upig).
- `perimeter.rs` — this one.

The core is ahead of the API, and an agent's picture of what this system can do comes from the API. The agent document tells it to ask the contract rather than a human; the contract cannot describe capability the handlers never reach.
design:
Do not start by wiring all of it. Decide first what §11 blocking should mean on the wire, because `blocks_period_reports` is a refusal and this API's refusals are now uniform: a blocked account presumably means the report answers for the other accounts and names this one as uncalculated, rather than failing the whole request. The doc comment already says the remainder must continue to be calculated, so the shape is a per-account exclusion carrying its reason, not a 4xx.

Note the interaction with iaam-upig, which surfaces the same negative-cash fact in the balances answer through `negative_cash()`. These must not become two independent notions of the same thing. `negative_cash()` is a snapshot; a span carries dates and a classification. If the perimeter is wired, the balances answer should read the span, and `negative_cash()` should be the span's input rather than a parallel path.

And note what classification requires: `TemporarySettlementDeficit` versus `UnsupportedMarginLiability` is decided from settlement terms and credit indicators, which is evidence, not owner judgement — so unlike iaam-d41s this needs no new owner input.
acceptance_criteria: Some request executes the perimeter assessment; a §11-blocking account is named as uncalculated in the report while the other accounts are still calculated; a test covers a blocking classification and a non-blocking one.
close_reason: perimeter::assess now runs on the balances answer. Blocking is a per-account marker inside a 200 with the refusing spans beside it, never a status code and never a withheld figure. negative_cash entries gained the span's dates and classification, additively and on the same key. The balances path moved to build_with, and /v1/reconciliation followed so the two routes cannot diverge.

title: The journal's correction mechanism is designed and reachable by nothing
description:
Reported as "no mechanism exists for correcting or retracting operations imported in error". The effect is right; the cause is narrower and much cheaper than that.

**The mechanism exists.** `crates/iaam-core/src/event/correction.rs` is titled "Corrections (§4.8): reversal plus replacement" and says exactly the right thing: the journal is append-only, so a correction does not erase the original — it adds an event that references it, and `resolve()` computes the effective set with reversed and replaced events excluded. `Relation` (crates/iaam-core/src/event/mod.rs:40) carries `Reversal { target }` and `Replacement { target }`, and projections are built from the resolved set.

**Nothing on the wire can produce one.** `grep -n relation crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs` returns nothing: no transport type carries a relation, so neither the operations ingest nor the journal-events ingest can submit a reversal or a replacement. The only route that emits one is the custody repair (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/custody_repair.rs:198), which is narrow by design — it retracts trades on an account whose broker access is gone.

So an operator who imports a month against the wrong account map is left where the reporter was: re-importing with the right map returns `duplicate` for every row, because the keys are derived from the raw rows and are correct; the wrong events stay; and the only remaining lever is destroying the database, which discards the correct entries with the incorrect ones. The design anticipated this and the API forgot to expose it.
design:
This is a wiring task with a policy question inside it, not a design task.

The wiring: carry `Relation` through the ingest transport so a submitted event can declare what it reverses or replaces. The core already validates and resolves; `resolve()` already errors on a dangling target and on conflicting replacements, so the failure modes are covered.

The policy question, which is the owner's: **who may correct.** A reversal rewrites what every downstream report says, and the agent document is explicit that the agent is an external client that does not write to the journal directly and does not decide the portfolio's shape. Custody repair already treats retraction as owner work — it demands `acknowledge_without_live_access` before retracting facts a later sync may not restore. A correction path should be at least that guarded.

The reporter's own suggestion — batch revocation keyed on the declared source, the `{account, channel}` pair `SubmitOperationsRequest` already carries — is worth weighing against per-event reversal: the reported failure is a whole import made wrong by one bad account map, and repairing it one event at a time through 177 reversals is a different ergonomics problem. But a batch retraction that is not itself a set of journal facts would break the append-only rule the design is built on. The likely answer is a batch **request** that writes per-event reversals.

Blocked in practice by the read gap: an operator cannot confirm which rows are wrong before reversing them.
acceptance_criteria: An owner can reverse or replace an ingested event through the API; the effective set excludes it exactly as correction::resolve already defines; a golden test covers an import made wrong by an account map and corrected without discarding the correct rows.
close_reason: Corrections got their own owner-only routes rather than a relation field on ingest, because may_submit admits an agent and four inputs converge on the ingest path. Per-event and per-import, both writing reversal facts, nothing deleted or mutated, validated through correction::resolve before the write. Also fixed: money_flow and account_balances folded the raw journal, so a reversal changed neither report — custody repair already wrote reversals, so that was live.

title: The journal has no read surface: what was imported becomes invisible at the row level
description:
An external agent imported 177 operations into a fresh instance, all accepted with verdict `provisional`, and then could not see what had landed. Verified: the GET routes this API serves are actions, instruments, instruments/{id}, reconciliation, classification-rules, category-groups, categories, category-rules, market prices/fx/key-rate, health, accounts, broker-access, tokens, and the three reports. There is no read for an operation, a journal event, or a document.

So an agent cannot answer "show me what was imported on a given day" or "show me the operation carrying this idempotency key". Every read surface is an aggregate: balances, flow, returns, reconciliation. A row goes in and stops being addressable.

This is not only an inconvenience. The agent document forbids arithmetic of the agent's own and tells it that every number in an answer must be present verbatim in the API's answer. When the owner asks about a single operation, the API has no answer to quote, and the agent's only remaining options are silence or the thing the document forbids.

It is also what blocks diagnosis of iaam-fixme-correction: an operator who suspects an import went in against the wrong accounts cannot confirm which rows are wrong before deciding what to do about them.
design:
Scope is the question, not feasibility. A list keyed on account and date range would answer the reported case; the idempotency key is the other natural handle, since it is the one value a caller already holds after an import. `SubmitOperationsRequest` also carries `source: Option<DeclaredSourceDto>` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:679), which would let a caller ask what one declared source put in.

Weigh against it that the journal holds the owner's whole financial history, that an agent token is deliberately less privileged than the owner's, and that a broad list route is the widest read surface this API would have. What the agent may read is a policy decision for the owner, not a default to be picked here.
acceptance_criteria: An agent can address an ingested operation by the handle it already holds, and can list what a given import put in, without reading an aggregate report.
close_reason: GET /v1/journal/events: optional filters by idempotency key, account with date range, and declared source; unfiltered listing allowed, keyset paging over the journal's own total order. Serves events, and the contract says so in those words. Relation is carried, so corrections are visible the day they land.

title: A balance computed from an unknown start is returned as a balance, and nothing asks for the start
description:
An external agent imported one month of operations into a fresh instance and got a **negative cash balance on a savings account**. A savings account cannot be overdrawn: that is an impossible state, not an incomplete one. Verified in the tree; two independent gaps produce it.

**Gap one — the queue asks for the closing point and never the opening one.** `provide_control_assertion_action` (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:700) hardcodes `let point = BalancePoint::Closing;`. `BalancePoint::Opening` exists and its own doc comment says what it is — "the state before the first event in the interval" (crates/iaam-core/src/reconciliation/claim.rs:62). `ActionKind` has ten variants and none of them concerns an opening balance. `EventKind::OpeningCash` and `OperationKindDto::OpeningCash` exist and the API accepts them (crates/iaam-core/src/event/kind.rs:225, crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:439). So the system holds both remedies and surfaces neither: an agent working the queue supplies a closing assertion, it is compared against a sum accumulated from zero, and the discrepancy it gets is not a discrepancy — it is the missing opening balance nobody asked for.

Note these are two different remedies and the fix must not conflate them: `opening_cash` is an **event** that puts money on the account, `BalancePoint::Opening` is an **assertion** about the balance before the interval. Which one the queue should ask for is the design question.

**Gap two — the report does not mark the number as unreconciled.** `BalanceCashDto` is `{ currency, amount }` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2145). Nothing on it says whether an opening point was ever asserted. `AccountBalanceDto` does carry a `reconciliation` block beside it, but that reports dimension statuses; it does not distinguish "a balance reconciled from a known start" from "a running sum from an unknown one", and the field is called `cash`, which invites reading it alone.

**Why the agent will not catch this by itself.** docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md says: never call `provisional` an error, it is an ordinary state of a correct journal. That instruction is right in general and here it disarms the agent — the impossible number arrives wearing the status the agent has been told not to flag.
design:
The core already computes the signal and no caller surfaces it. `Balances::negative_cash()` exists (crates/iaam-core/src/projection/balances.rs:127) with the comment 'At stage 1 this is not an error: a negative margin balance is a liability'; its only consumer is the returns computation (crates/iaam-core/src/returns/mod.rs:2207). `PerimeterFinding::UnclassifiedNegativeCash` exists too (crates/iaam-core/src/perimeter.rs:61). Neither reaches the balances report or the action queue.

That reframes the cost. The report does not need a new invariant — it needs to carry what the core already knows, plus a marker for 'no opening point asserted for the period before the first operation'. Note that a negative balance is legitimate on a margin account, which is exactly why the core refuses to call it an error; the report must therefore state the fact and let the reader judge, rather than refuse.

Two candidate answers, and they are not exclusive — the reporter asked for either:
(a) the queue asks for the opening point before it asks for the closing one, so the second question is never put before the first is answered;
(b) the balances report marks a balance unreconciled when no opening assertion covers the period before the first operation.

(b) is the one that makes the impossible number visible to a reader who is not working the queue at all, so it is the one that closes the reported failure. (a) prevents the phantom discrepancy that follows. Both are wanted; (b) first.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh instance with one month imported and no opening assertion returns its cash figure marked as computed from an unasserted start; the action queue asks for the opening point before the closing one; a golden test covers the fresh-import case end to end.
close_reason: Every cash figure carries whether its start was asserted, on the figure itself, unconditionally — not only on anomalous rows. The answer gained negative_cash from Balances::negative_cash(), stated as a fact and never refused. The queue asks the opening point before the closing one, both now RequiredForGoal. Also fixed a defect present on main: record_owner_balance wrote its assertion undated, so one owner-recorded balance made every reconciliation, balances and returns report 500 — verified by reverting the line.

title: The surface says investment accounting; the API serves personal finance too, and an agent draws the boundary in the wrong place
description:
An external agent read the contract and the agent document, concluded the system was investment-only, and told the owner his personal expenses did not belong here. It was wrong, and it took a human correction to see it — which is precisely the failure the bootstrap in docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md exists to prevent.

Verified against the tree:

- `info.description` is "Investment accounting. Stage 1: cash flows and pre-tax XIRR." (crates/iaam-server/src/openapi.rs:70). It names one half. A client that reads the title, then meets `buy`, `sell`, `instrument` and `custody` among the first operation types, stops looking. `CategoryGroupDto.is_income` (dto.rs:4008), `source_category` on an operation (dto.rs:473) and `went_out_by_category` on the money-flow report (dto.rs:1958) are all there, below the fold, after the framing is already set.
- `grep -c categor docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md` returns **0**. The document is written end to end in investment vocabulary — portfolio, contour, contribution, return, XIRR. An agent reading it in the intended order, meaning before the contract, learns nothing about spending at all.
- The bootstrap actions are `create_first_account`, `create_first_contour`, `start_account_import` (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:36-38). Nothing surfaces a category or a bank CSV as a first step, although both are first-class: `EventKind::Refund` is a domain variant (crates/iaam-core/src/event/kind.rs:174, schema version 11) and a T-Bank CSV importer ships as a skill.

README.md calls the project «учёт инвестиций» in its first line, which is consistent with the framing and part of the same picture.
design:
The reporter explicitly did not ask for a rename or a rewritten skill, and this bead does not propose either. The observation is that the boundary between the investment half and the personal-finance half is invisible from outside, so an agent will draw it, and draw it wrongly.

Three surfaces could carry that boundary, in ascending order of cost:

1. `info.description` — one sentence naming both halves and how they relate. Cheapest, and it is the string that framed the reporter.
2. The agent document — a section on what a category is and how spending relates to return, in the same register as the existing sections. This is the owner's design artefact and the change is his to approve, not an agent's to make.
3. The action queue — a bootstrap action for the spending half, so the queue an agent is told to work does not describe only one half of the system.

Whether the answer is all three, one, or a fourth thing is a design decision. Do not implement without the owner's direction.
acceptance_criteria: An agent that reads only the discovery document, the contract's info block and the agent document can state that the system tracks personal spending as well as investments, without being corrected by a human.
close_reason: info.description names both halves; the agent document's own description and heading say personal accounting; a new section after the contour explains what a category is and states the return corollary in the only wording that is true. The action-queue leg was split off as iaam-z7q6 because it needs the diagnostic split at its source, not a relabel.

title: Extractor rejections bypass ApiError: the contract declares 422 JSON, the server returns 400 text/plain
description:
Routes taking `Query<T>` or `Json<T>` return axum's own rejection: HTTP 400 with a text/plain body such as "Failed to deserialize query string: missing field `contour`". Only hand-parsed bodies produce the documented shape (`create_instrument`, crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs:259, via `invalid_field`).

Two consequences, the second the serious one:

1. An agent parsing errors programmatically must handle two encodings.
2. `grep -c 'status = 400' crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs` is 0, while 16 `Json<T>` routes and every `Query<T>` route can return one. The OpenAPI document promises `422 ApiError` and the instance serves an undeclared `400 text/plain`. The agent skill instructs agents to read the contract instead of asking what a refusal looks like; here the contract lies.
design: Map both rejection kinds into `ApiError` with `code`, `message`, `field`, `expected`, `actual`, so a missing or unparseable query parameter is indistinguishable in shape from a rejected body field. Either a custom extractor wrapper or axum's `FromRequest`-with-rejection. Then declare the status on every affected operation. Reported by an external agent exercising the live API.
acceptance_criteria: Every 4xx from the server has content-type application/json and deserialises as ApiError; a contract test asserts it for at least one Query route and one Json route; OpenAPI declares the status on affected operations.
close_reason: ApiQuery/ApiJson/ApiPath/ApiBytes give every 4xx an ApiError JSON body; 422 for deserialisation, with 400/413/415 kept where 422 would misdescribe, all declared in the contract. Merged in api-error-envelope; 1848 workspace tests pass.

title: Provisioning through the CLI seeds the operation-kind dictionary
description:
`SqliteAdapter::add_access` (`crates/iaam-app/src/adapters/sqlite.rs:550-572`)
seeds the broker operation-kind dictionary in the same blocking task that stores
the credential. Its own comment says why: access set up without a dictionary
rejects the import.

`provision.rs::add_broker_access`, the CLI path, writes `insert_broker_access`
directly and never seeds. The word "dictionary" does not appear in the file.

While both paths existed this was an inconsistency. With the HTTP route removed
(iaam-phym) the CLI is the only way to provision, so every newly provisioned
broker gets no dictionary — and the contract test that would have caught it,
`provisioning_an_access_fills_the_channel_dictionary`, was deleted with the route
it exercised. Its comment is the warning worth keeping: a missing synonym breaks
no obvious case, and half the export stops parsing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Provisioning through the CLI seeds the operation-kind dictionary for the broker
  it provisions, from `iaam_broker::operation_kind::seed_for`.
- Storing the credential and seeding the dictionary succeed or fail together. A
  credential stored without its dictionary is the state this bead exists to
  prevent, and a crash between two writes would recreate it.
- A broker with no known dictionary is refused with a message naming that as the
  reason, as the application path already does.
- Replacing a credential does not re-seed pointlessly, and does not lose an
  existing dictionary.
- A test proves the dictionary exists after provisioning, and names one synonym
  rather than only a count — the deleted contract test checked
  `OPERATION_TYPE_DIV_EXT` for exactly that reason.
close_reason: Both provisioning paths now call one store operation that writes the credential and seeds the operation-kind dictionary in a single Immediate transaction; a broker with no known dictionary is refused by name; rotation leaves the dictionary alone. The dictionary-less insert survives for fixtures and says in its own doc comment that it is not for provisioning. Found by reviewing what the removed HTTP route did that the CLI did not.

title: No HTTP route accepts a broker credential
description:
ADR-0003 states the boundary absolutely: no credential but its own access token
ever reaches an agent, and credential SUBMISSION leaves HTTP while status and
revocation stay. `iaam broker access add` shipped and reads the token from stdin.

The unsafe paths were never removed:

- `POST /v1/broker-access` takes `AddBrokerAccessRequest.token`
  (`crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2348`, handler `routes.rs:1116`).
- `PUT /v1/brokers/{broker}/access` takes `BrokerAccessUpdateRequest`
  (`routes.rs:989`).

Both are registered (`lib.rs:68`, `lib.rs:106`). Marking the field `password` and
`write_only` in the schema keeps it out of responses; it does not stop the
plaintext travelling to the API through whatever holds the owner-scope token —
which, by ADR-0003, is the agent.

So the boundary is documented, the safe path exists, and the unsafe one is still
open. Adding a door does not close the other one, and the close reason on
iaam-iw9s claimed otherwise.

Found by an adversarial review of the E9.T2 spec, not by a test — nothing asserts
the absence of a credential-accepting route.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Neither route accepts a token. Credential submission and rotation exist only
  in the CLI.
- Non-secret operations stay over HTTP as ADR-0003 requires: listing broker
  access, its environment and status, and revoking it. Revocation is not
  submission and must keep working.
- The request DTOs lose the secret field, and the OpenAPI document no longer
  advertises a route that takes one.
- A contract test asserts that no route accepts a credential field — by shape,
  so that a future route reintroducing one fails rather than passing unnoticed.
- `docs/deployment.md` and any guidance describing the HTTP submission path are
  corrected.
close_reason: POST /v1/broker-access and PUT /v1/brokers/{broker}/access are gone with their DTOs, components, registrations and tests. Listing and revoking stay, as ADR-0003 requires. iaam broker access rotate replaces PUT, reading the token from stdin. A contract test walks every request body in the generated document and refuses a password or write-only field by shape, with its limit stated: a credential typed as an ordinary string would pass.

title: The agent skill stops narrating routes and stops lying about 501
description:
`docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md` tells agents that classification-rule routes, broker
sync and `POST /v1/instruments` answer `501` (lines 47, 82, 256, 294). The
handlers are implemented. An agent that believes the document does not do work
the system can do — the exact harm E9 exists to remove, shipped and live.

The lie is deleted immediately. The reduction follows the computed queue and
cannot outrun it: a section is removed when something computed answers it, not
before.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every `501` claim is checked against the handlers and corrected or deleted.
  Where a route genuinely is unimplemented, the document says which and is
  checked by something, or it will rot again.
- Sections describing how to behave in states production never constructs
  (`needs_reconciliation`, `needs_classification`) are removed or rewritten to
  what actually occurs.
- What stays is what no state can compute: what a contour is, why owner-stated
  evidence is not independent, why the agent is an external client, how to read a
  report's meaning. Prose about meaning, not about calls.
- What goes, as each becomes computable: hardcoded paths and methods,
  required-field inventories, first-time setup ordering, verdict-to-call tables,
  instructions to poll a specific endpoint.
- The end state is a bootstrap pointer: discover `/v1`, read the OpenAPI
  document, query `/v1/actions`. If it still narrates route availability, E9 has
  failed.
design:
POLICY-CHANGE JUSTIFICATION (check-diff-lint.sh).

Files touched that the guard classes as quality policy:
  scripts/check-agent-skill.sh  (new)
  .github/workflows/ci.yml      (adds the step)

Net effect is strictly MORE checking, not less. The acceptance criterion of this
bead requires the 501 claim to be 'checked by something, or it will rot again',
and a corrected sentence is not that. The new guard refuses a versioned route
path, an HTTP method written as an instruction, and an HTTP status code anywhere
in docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md, so the document cannot make an availability claim
at all. It checks shapes, needs no list of routes, and therefore cannot itself go
stale when the API changes — the same construction as the privacy guard. It
self-probes all three shapes.

Proven both directions: passes on the reduced document, and refuses the previous
one with findings on every 501 line.
close_reason: The document names no route, method or status code, and scripts/check-agent-skill.sh refuses one if it appears. Every 501 claim checked against the handlers: all four were false, and nothing in the codebase has ever returned 501. Verified the guard refuses the previous document and passes the reduced one.

title: The CLI keeps the secrets, as subcommands rather than environment variables
description:
ADR-0003. The owner's console surface exists but is expressed as environment
variables consumed at process start: `IAAM_ISSUE_OWNER_TOKEN`,
`IAAM_ADD_BROKER_ACCESS`, `IAAM_GENERATE_BROKER_KEY`, and rotation through
`IAAM_BROKER_KEY_OLD_FILE` / `IAAM_BROKER_KEY_NEW_FILE`. Provisioning a broker
means restarting the server with a variable set.

The CLI is what keeps a secret out of the model's context. That is its whole
remit, and the boundary is secrets and the trust root — NOT "initial setup",
which has no edge and would creep until the CLI is a second application.

## Claiming moves here, and the one-time code is retired

`POST /v1/claim`, `CLAIM_LIFETIME` and `accept_claim` exist for one reason: HTTP
needs a proof of console access, and a code read from the console is that proof.
A CLI has console access by definition and has nothing to prove. Removing the
route removes a bootstrap secret that would otherwise have to travel through
whoever calls the API — which the owner has ruled out absolutely: nothing but its
own access token ever reaches an agent.

It also removes the timing difference between an armed and a claimed instance:
`accept_claim` (`crates/iaam-server/src/claim.rs:54`) hashes a submitted code
only while a claim is pending.

E9.T1 depends on this removal: while the route exists, the discovery answer
either advertises it — routing a secret through the agent — or lies by omission.

## What does NOT move

Non-secret operations do not follow their secret siblings out of HTTP. Broker
access status and revocation, and token metadata and revocation, stay callable:
a surface must be able to show what exists and to withdraw it. What leaves is
credential submission — the plaintext.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Real subcommands replace the provisioning environment variables: `claim`,
  issue and revoke a token, generate and rotate the broker key, submit and rotate
  broker credentials.
- Starting the server is a subcommand too, so no invocation silently provisions
  as a side effect of running the service.
- `iaam claim` creates the owner through the store, as `provision.rs` already
  does for broker access, and prints the token once.
- `POST /v1/claim`, the claim code and its lifetime are deleted, along with the
  startup console print that arms it. The OpenAPI document no longer offers it.
- A secret is never printed back, never logged, never returned — the present
  guarantee in `provision.rs` is preserved, not weakened.
- Nothing that is not a secret or the trust root moves into the CLI. Accounts,
  contours, categories, balances and imports stay with the agent.
- `docs/deployment.md` documents the mechanism being replaced and is rewritten
  with it.
- The removed variables fail loudly for one release rather than being silently
  ignored: an operator who sets an old variable is told the subcommand.

## The removal surface, enumerated

A partial deletion leaves a dangling reference that compiles or a document that
still tells an operator to read a code. Every site:

- `crates/iaam-server/src/claim.rs` — the whole module.
- `crates/iaam-server/src/lib.rs` — `pub mod claim`, the `ClaimCode` import,
  `ServerState.claim` and its methods, and the route registration (~line 170).
- `crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs:1195` — the handler and its refusal helper.
- `crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2416` — `ClaimRequest`, its custom `Debug` and
  its tests.
- `crates/iaam-server/src/openapi.rs` — the import and component registration.
- `crates/iaam-server/tests/contract.rs` — claim helpers and cases (~762, ~2462),
  replaced by an assertion that the route is gone.
- `crates/iaam-bootstrap/src/main.rs:249` — arming and printing the code at
  startup.
- `docs/deployment.md:47` — and the surrounding first-token section.
- `crates/iaam-app/src/tokens.rs:39` — a comment that still names the claim code.

## Claiming must be atomic

`issue_owner_token` reads `sole_owner()` and then issues
(`crates/iaam-bootstrap/src/main.rs:318-338`). There is no single-owner
constraint in the token table — the store has a `SoleOwner::Several` arm
precisely because this went wrong once before, as the function's own comment
records. Two `iaam claim` processes racing would each see `None` and create a
different owner, and the second owner's portfolio would appear empty while the
first token still worked.

The subcommand therefore claims inside one transaction, or under an exclusive
lock, and a test runs two claims concurrently and proves exactly one succeeds.
notes: CORRECTION to the close reason. This task added the CLI's safe path for broker credentials; it did NOT remove the HTTP routes that still accept a plaintext token — POST /v1/broker-access and PUT /v1/brokers/{broker}/access. The close reason implied the credential boundary of ADR-0003 had shipped, and it has not. Tracked as iaam-phym, found by an adversarial review rather than by a test, because nothing asserts the absence of a credential-accepting route.
close_reason: Two workers: subcommands replacing the provisioning environment variables (serve, claim, token issue, broker key generate/rotate, broker access add), with the old variables refusing to run and naming their replacement; then the removal of POST /v1/claim with its one-time code, module, state, DTO, OpenAPI component and tests, replaced by one contract test asserting 404 and absence from the document. Claiming decides and creates under BEGIN IMMEDIATE — issue_owner_token read sole_owner and then issued, and nothing constrained a single owner. The broker token now comes from stdin rather than argv. docs/deployment.md rewritten. Follow-up filed as iaam-odqr: claim_owner assembles a token record itself because the port is not transaction-aware, which is a second implementation of credential issuance.
