title: A directionless row settled as an internal transfer derives its direction from a guess
description:
In `movement_of` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/import_session.rs), a row whose source stated **no** direction but whose counterparty resolves to one of the owner's own accounts gets `Movement::Out` derived purely from `to != row.account`.

That is the guess `question_for`'s own doc comment refuses one function away — «the answer would be recorded and the guess would be made anyway, one step further along». And it is wrong in both directions: `Answer::ReceivedFromOwnAccount { from }` also encodes the far side as `to`, so a directionless row settled by such a rule derives `Out` for money that arrived.

Pre-existing, and iaam-f8d3 made it more reachable: broadening resolution from titles to identities and aliases means more rows reach this path. Found and deliberately left alone by the agent that did f8d3, rather than expanding that change's scope silently.
design:
Probably `Question::UnresolvedDirection` when `row.movement()` is `None` and the classification is `InternalTransfer` — the row is asked rather than settled, which is what every other directionless outcome already does. `ExternalFlow` is the existing precedent: it carries no direction, so a directionless row settled as one is still asked.

Check first whether `Answer::ReceivedFromOwnAccount` should stop encoding the far side in a field named `to`. If the answer type distinguished the two directions structurally, this bug would have been unwritable, and fixing the derivation without fixing the encoding leaves the trap set for the next reader.

title: The queue tells an agent nothing can start an import, and two routes can
description:
`start_account_import_action` (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:1485) is built by `blocked_action` — `ActionState::Blocked`, target `None` — and its reason reads: «Account … has no business facts; import a statement or connect a broker. Import is continuous and never complete. **No operation in this API fetches the document.**»

The last sentence is true and it is not the claim the state makes. `ActionState::Blocked` is documented as «no operation in this API is available for this item» (actions.rs:88). Two are: `POST /v1/import-sessions` opens the session that the first remedy consists of, and `POST /v1/brokers/{broker}/sync` is the second remedy entire. What has no operation is fetching the statement out of the bank — a step outside the API, not a missing route.

So an agent walking the queue is told that nothing here can help with the single most important next step, and stops. Found while auditing all fourteen action kinds for iaam-ht3l.

This is very likely the root of iaam-51c0: a reviewer who ran a whole import without finding the assessment reached the session by reading the OpenAPI document, because the queue disowned the route.
design:
It becomes `NeedsOwnerInput` with an `Options` target — the variant iaam-ht3l just added — naming `open_import_session` and `sync_broker`, each with its own request plan. The broker option needs the broker; the session option needs whatever `POST /v1/import-sessions` requires.

Keep the sentence about fetching the document. It is the honest part: the owner does have to obtain the statement himself, and the queue should say so while still naming what to call once he has it.

Precedent for the promotion is recorded in this file already: `undecomposed_outflows_action`'s doc comment explains why that item was moved out of `Blocked` for exactly this reason.
close_reason:
start_account_import is now NeedsOwnerInput with an Options target naming open_import_session and sync_broker, each with its own request plan. The sentence keeps its honest half — the owner must obtain the statement himself, no operation here downloads it — and now also names what to call once he has.

The fix surfaced a latent gap in the contract test rather than only a stale belief: every_action_request_schema_required_input_is_advertised_as_missing understood only 'none' and 'operation' targets, so it read requestSchema off an options target and got null. Every alternative resolution was going unchecked — the exact failure Options exists to end. It now sweeps option by option.

Consequence worth knowing: frontier emits no Blocked item at all any more. Every blocked diagnostic is carried by reports and broker sync, not by GET /v1/actions. Recorded in the contract test's doc comment rather than left to make its blocked branch silently vacuous.

Merged; make check exits 0 on the merged branch.

title: Nothing in a report says how far it can be trusted; the client assembles that from four fields
description:
A QA run through accounts → contour → import session → assessment → answer → commit → balances reported the same difficulty four times, and it is one difficulty:

- `readiness: ready` means the commit will not be refused. It does not mean the import was fully understood.
- `GET /v1/reports/balances` answers 200 with ordinary rows while `population.completeness` is `undecided` — in that run, `covered=3, outside=15`. `population` is the last top-level field, after `accounts` and `negative_cash`, so the figures read as complete unless the block is checked deliberately.
- `cash.amount` under `opening: unasserted` is a running sum from an unknown start and is not a balance. The DTO says so precisely (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2637). The endpoint is called balances and the field is called amount.
- `cross_source_matching.unmatched` looks like unresolved transfers (see the separate bead).

Every one of these facts is published, correctly, and none is missing. The client still has to reconstruct «how much of this answer do I believe» from four fields in three shapes, and a client that reads only the numbers gets a confident wrong impression. The reviewer's summary: «ready ≠ complete, 200 ≠ confirmed balance, amount ≠ balance under unasserted opening».
design:
Resist inventing a trust score. A number the owner cannot check is exactly what PairingEvidenceDto refused to publish, and for the same reason.

What is wanted is one statement per report, assembled by the core from facts that already exist, saying what would have to be true for the figures to be complete and which of those are not:

    confidence: { complete: bool, caveats: [ { kind, subject, detail } ] }

with kinds drawn from what is already computed — accounts outside no scope, cash figures on an unasserted opening, unrepaired coverage gaps, unanswered questions. Every caveat must point at the field a client can read to see the same thing, so this stays a summary and never a second source of truth.

Two constraints on placement. It goes **first** in the response, not last: a caveat published after the figures has already lost to the reader who stopped at the figures. And it is computed in the core beside the numbers, per commit 54fc437 — a summary of a report assembled by the transport can disagree with the report.

Related, not duplicate: iaam-f5e7 does the same job for the action queue (which goal is this item required for). This one is about the reports. They should use the same vocabulary of goals.
close_reason:
Each report opens with a register of what its figures do not account for: {goal, complete, caveats[{kind, subject, detail, see}]}, applied to balances, flow and returns. Nine caveat kinds, each derived from a computation the reports already performed — no new fold anywhere.

Four decisions beyond the brief, all improvements on it:

- complete is not a stored field. ReportConfidence holds {goal, caveats} privately and complete() is caveats.is_empty(), so there is no constructor that can assert completeness beside a non-empty register. The required invariant is enforced by the type rather than by a check that can be forgotten.
- detail and see are constants of the kind, not strings a caller passes. A Caveat is only {kind, subject}. Nothing of the report is interpolated into the prose, so the summary cannot restate a figure wrongly and no caveat can point where its fact is not.
- negative_cash is deliberately not a caveat: a negative balance is a fact the answer states and the reader judges, it does not make the figures incomplete, and a register firing on every overdraft would fire on almost every report. Where it does make a period incomplete, §11 says so through period_reports, which is a caveat. Pinned by its own test.
- The contract test asserts on raw bytes rather than serde_json::Value, because Value sorts keys and first-ness is only checkable on the wire. Its pre-fix output is the exact shape the QA run described.

The core-computation constraint drove a real move: ten report types migrated from scenarios::reports into a new iaam-core/src/report/, re-exported under their old paths so nothing else churned. make arch passes.

/v1/reconciliation deliberately left out: it is per-account by request parameter, so there is no population to be partial about, and its gaps array already is the register.

Merged; make check exits 0.

title: cross_source_matching.unmatched holds every cash movement, and its name promises transfers
description:
`leg_of_event` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/transfer_pairing.rs:237) turns **every** `CashOut` and `CashIn` with a posting date into a `TransferLeg`. `propose` then reports as `unmatched` every leg nothing paired with. For an ordinary import with no transfers in it at all, that is every row.

A QA run on a synthetic contour got `facts=5, candidates=0, unmatched=5` — the five ordinary deposits and withdrawals it had just imported — and could not tell whether something had gone wrong.

The information is right and the intent is deliberate: the module doc (transfer_pairing.rs:20) argues that a leg dropped from the answer is a leg the owner reads as external flow by default, which is the defect rather than the fix. The naming is what misleads. A block called `cross_source_matching` containing `unmatched: Vec<TransferLegDto>` reads as «transfers we failed to match». What it means is «cash movements with no counterpart proposed», and for a grocery purchase that is the correct and permanent state.
design:
Do not filter the list. Completeness is the point, and the argument for it in the module doc is sound.

Two cheaper fixes, and they compose:

- **Say it in the contract.** `CrossSourceMatchingDto.unmatched` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs) needs a doc comment stating that an ordinary one-sided movement belongs here permanently and that an empty `candidates` with a full `unmatched` is the normal shape of an import containing no transfers. The type names carry an implication the prose has to withdraw.
- **Rank it, once there is something to rank by.** After iaam-f8d3 wires the owner's transfer-partner statements into the import, a leg on an account he has declared a partner for is materially more likely to be half of a transfer than a card payment is. That is a real signal and the honest place to spend it: order or flag `unmatched`, still publishing all of it.

Renaming the field is the third option and probably wrong — `unmatched` is accurate, it is `TransferLeg` that overclaims. If anything is renamed it is the type.
close_reason:
Prose, plus one rename. No behaviour changed: leg_of_event untouched, nothing filtered.

The domain type TransferLeg became CashLeg. The overclaim had a source and a copy — the copy is the response block's prose, which prose can withdraw; the source is the type name, from which every future reader re-derives the wrong meaning before reaching any comment, including whoever next feels the urge to 'fix' unmatched by filtering it. The domain type is workspace-internal with no serde name and no schema, so the rename is free; TransferLegDto stays, because it is published in the OpenAPI schema and renaming the wire would break clients for a word. The divergence is documented on both sides, and a glossary row added per the repository's own rule about domain terms.

CrossSourceMatchingDto now states that candidates: [] beside a full unmatched is the normal shape of an import containing no transfers, and that for a card payment or a salary unmatched is a correct and permanent state with nothing for the owner to do. ImportPlanDto::cross_source_matching — the field the QA run actually read — says the same in one line. Merged; lint and both crates green.

title: There is no report of what the owner owns, by class of asset
description:
The reports are flow, returns, balances and reconciliation. `GET /v1/reports/balances` answers per account and currency — `BalancesReportDto.accounts` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2525) — with no total and no grouping.

The owner's primary question is not answered by any of them: how much is on deposit, how much on savings accounts, how much on ordinary and card accounts, how much in the wallet, how much invested, and what the whole is worth. Assembling it from the balances report means grouping accounts by reading their titles, which is exactly the guess this repository refuses everywhere else.

Two open beads already say the product is described as narrower than it is — iaam-wu9n and iaam-2wgj. This is the report that half is missing.
design:
Two parts, and the second cannot start until the first is decided.

**The class.** An account needs a class of asset — cash, savings, term deposit, wallet, brokerage — supplied by the owner, never inferred. This overlaps iaam-34f3 (external identity) and collides with iaam-d41s, whose design argues **against** a kind taxonomy on the grounds that a kind enum invites every later feature to branch on it, citing InstrumentKind as the cautionary precedent. That argument was made about a different need — knowing which negative balances are impossible — and it stands for that need. This need is different: a grouping in a report is not a branch in a rule, and the owner supplies it directly. Reconcile the two explicitly in the ADR iaam-34f3 already calls for rather than adding a field that contradicts a recorded decision.

**The report.** Given a class, the snapshot is a fold the balances report already performs, regrouped: class → currency → total, plus the securities positions valued the way the returns report values them. It must carry the same `population` block the balances report carries — an asset total that silently omits an account is worse than no total — and it must state which figures are valued from market data and as of when.

Cards are a non-issue here once iaam-34f3 lands: two bindings over one underlying account are one account with two aliases, and the snapshot counts it once. Today they would be two accounts and the total would be wrong twice.
notes:
Owner's position (2026-09-03): iaam should carry both the abstract per-class statistic and the detailed one.

Agreed, with three refinements that narrow the work:

1. One report at two folds, not two reports. Precedent: commit 54fc437, «money is summed in the core, not in the session» — the architecture guard caught a fold done outside the core. The class total and the per-account rows must come from the same projection, or they can disagree and nothing says which is wrong.

2. The proposed enum is half redundant. `Balances` already splits cash from positions structurally (crates/iaam-core/src/projection/balances.rs:41) and `AccountBalanceDto` publishes both (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2586). `brokerage` and `security_position` need no declaration — a position on an instrument is what the journal records. What cannot be derived is which **cash** account is a deposit, a savings account, a card account or a wallet. The declaration shrinks to a label on cash, four values.

   This nearly dissolves the collision with iaam-d41s. Its objection was that a kind enum invites every later feature to branch on it. A label consumed by one report's grouping is not a branch. State the condition in the ADR: it stays a label. A rule branching on it later is evidence the objection was right, not licence to grow the enum.

3. The hard parts are population and valuation, not classification.
   - Population: a total that silently omits an account is worse than no total. Carry `PopulationDto` (dto.rs:2230) and put `completeness` — including `undecided` — on the total line.
   - Valuation: cash is exact, positions are as of a quote. The two halves and the price date are stated before the total, or a market-dependent figure reads as a bank figure.

Sequencing: the cash label does not depend on external identity and can be specified in parallel with the ADR. What the snapshot does depend on is the aliases half of iaam-34f3 — until two card bindings are one account, the total double-counts.

title: RequiredForGoal names no goal, so the queue reads as a gate on everything
description:
`ActionCategory` has four values and only `Blocking` says what it stops (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:71). `RequiredForGoal` names no goal. `resolve_transfer_relationships` and `account_scope_undecided` both carry it, and a client walking the queue cannot tell that the first is required for flow and returns while the second is required for every report there is.

The consequence is not hypothetical: an external reviewer read the queue as a precondition on the whole import and proposed reordering the workflow around it. The code does not agree — `account_balances` (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/reports.rs:562) folds journal events against a contour and never reads a transfer statement, and `plan_session`'s readiness (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/import_session.rs:906) turns on open questions and pairing candidates, not on partner statements. Nothing was ever blocked. The queue merely failed to say so.
design:
Give the category its object: `RequiredForGoal { goal }`, where the goal is one of the answers the owner can ask for — asset snapshot and balances, money flow, returns, reconciliation. Then a client can ask «what stands between me and a balance sheet» and get a shorter list than «what stands between me and everything».

Mapping as the code stands:

- `account_scope_undecided` — every goal. An account in no contour appears in no report.
- `resolve_transfer_relationships` — flow, returns, reconciliation. Not balances: a leg folds into its own account's balance whether or not its partner is known.
- `answer_classification_question` — every goal, since the row records nothing until answered.
- the reconciliation and decomposition items — their own goals already.

Note the ordering constraint: this is worth doing after iaam-f8d3, which may change what the transfer statement is required for by making it required for anything at all.
close_reason:
ActionCategory::RequiredForGoal(ReportGoals) — a four-bit set over asset_snapshot, money_flow, returns, reconciliation; published as ActionDto.goals, always present, [] for non-required categories. ActionKind::goals() is an exhaustive match, so a fifteenth kind is a compile error rather than a stale table, and Action::new refuses a required action naming no goal.

Two design traps avoided: PartialOrd/Ord dropped from ActionCategory, because a derived order over a payload variant would have ordered two required items by their bit patterns and sort_actions would silently have adopted that as the queue's order (urgency is now an explicit rank()); and the test restates the expected goal set in its own exhaustive match rather than reading it back from ActionKind::goals, since a test that asks the table what the table says passes for any table.

Six corrections to the mapping I supplied, each with code evidence: create_first_account is Blocking not required; undecomposed_outflows is Recommended and the other two flow diagnostics Informational, so none carries goals; resolve_transfer_relationships is not required for reconciliation, because confirm_journal_pairing replaces two events with a CashTransfer carrying the same legs and ObservedTotals accumulates from legs, so nothing it observes moves; provide_control_assertion is required for asset_snapshot and not returns; create_first_contour and account_scope_undecided are not required for reconciliation, because scenarios::reconciliation::report takes an account and never resolves a contour; possible_duplicate_undecided is every goal, because DedupDecision::records_the_row is true for it and the row may be the same money counted twice.

Merged as fc01d35; make check exits 0.

title: The import assessment exists and nothing points a client at it
description:
`GET /v1/import-sessions/{session}/assessment` already answers, section by section, what an external reviewer asked for as a wishlist: `source_inventory.accounts`, `account_resolution.{resolved,missing,conflicting}`, `scope_assessment`, `interpretation.open_questions`, `cross_source_matching`, `commit_delta.{facts,duplicates,retained_unrecorded}`, `readiness`. He ran a whole import without finding it and wrote the wishlist instead.

Nothing led him there. The action queue never names the assessment; the session responses do not link it; the commit route accepts a `revision` whose only source is the assessment, and does not say so where a client would look.
design:
Cheapest fix first: when a session has rows, emit an action — or at least name the assessment in the session response — so a client walking the queue reaches it. `ImportSessionDto` could carry the assessment's path the way the commit route carries `revision`.

Then the documentation half: the import walkthrough in docs/ should show open → add rows → assess → answer → commit, with the assessment as the step that is read before anything is written. Check whether the tbank-csv-import skill does the assess call; if it does not, that is the same gap in the other surface.

title: An account has no identity outside iaam, so every importer keeps its own map
description:
`AccountDto` is `{id, title, institution}` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2899). Nothing in it says which account at the institution it is. A client re-importing next month has two options: keep a side file mapping the source's identifier to the uuid, or encode the identifier in `title`. Both are what the import skills do today via `--account-map`, and both break silently when the source renames something.

There is also no model for a card. Two cards over one underlying account are, to this API, either one account (and the source's two identifiers must be merged by the client) or two (and the balance is counted twice). An external reviewer hit exactly this: two bindings, one underlying account.

Related to iaam-d41s, which wants an account kind for a different reason.
design:
The privacy convention (CLAUDE.md) forbids the owner's account number entering the repository — but not the database, which is his. Still, the safe shape is a fingerprint the client computes, not the number:

    provider: String            // `tbank`, `broker-x` — the client's own label
    provider_account_id: String // opaque to iaam, unique within provider
    aliases: Vec<String>        // further identifiers the source uses for the same account

with (provider, provider_account_id) unique per owner, and an upsert-by-external-identity route so a re-import finds the account it made last time instead of minting a second.

Cards are the harder half and may deserve their own bead: an `alias` list is enough to fold two card numbers onto one account, but not enough to say a binding expired. Decide whether iaam needs binding lifecycle at all — the reporting perimeter is accounts, and a card is a way to reach one.

An ADR is warranted: this is hard to reverse and it puts source-shaped identifiers in the store for the first time.
close_reason:
Migration 0020: provider, provider_account_id, cash_class on accounts plus an account_aliases table. The identity index is partial — it binds only rows carrying both halves — so two identity-less accounts are never merged and no existing database fails to migrate. create_account upserts inside an Immediate transaction, because the lookup and insert are check-then-act and two concurrent imports would otherwise both mint.

A create whose identity matches but whose title differs returns the existing account unchanged, with 200 rather than 201: a title is a display name, so repeating an identity under a new one is not a rename and must not silently overwrite what the owner reads, and 201 for an account minted on an earlier call is a claim the client cannot check. The call is idempotent, not an update.

The cash class lives in the storage adapter, not iaam-core — the core is where rules live, and a label no rule may read has no business being reachable from one. brokerage and security_position are absent by design and tested as refused. The prohibition is written on the enum and names the one branch that would be reached for first: which negative balances are impossible must not be derived from it.

Two additions beyond the brief, both justified: PUT /v1/accounts/{id}/aliases, because without it aliases could only be stated at creation while the two-cards case normally arrives afterwards; and a pair check that provider and provider_account_id are both present or both absent, which never inspects either value and does not echo the identifier back in its refusal.

Left as scoped: resolve_counterparty still matches titles (iaam-f8d3), nothing groups by class (iaam-tgcy), no export redaction (out of scope per the ADR). Merged; make check exits 0.

title: Which accounts money moves between is asked of accounts already ruled outside
description:
`frontier` filters `ResolveTransferRelationships` on `transfer_relationships_gap` alone (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:1165) — a statement exists or it does not. Scope is not consulted, so an account the owner has explicitly ruled outside the perimeter, with a reason, still raises the item, as does an expired card binding once bindings exist at all.

An external reviewer importing two institutions got one such question per account and could not tell which of them he was obliged to answer.

Not obviously wrong: an outside account can still be the far side of a transfer from an inside one, which is exactly what the item exists to discover. But the queue does not say so, and «required for a goal» on an account the owner has ruled out of every report is at best unexplained.
design:
Decide first, then code. Either

- outside accounts are still asked, and the reason says why (`this account is outside the perimeter, but money may still cross it`); or
- outside accounts are not asked, and the partner statement is inferred from the inside account's side.

The second is cheaper for the owner and loses nothing: a transfer has two ends and one of them is inside. Prefer it unless the pairing code needs both statements.

Also missing: a way to answer several of these at once. Twelve accounts is twelve calls.
close_reason:
An account ruled outside every contour no longer raises the item; Undecided still does. Scope moved into transfer_relationships_eligibility rather than the gap: the gap is 'has he answered', this is 'is the question worth asking'.

Three reasons the suppression is lossless, verified rather than assumed: (1) the harm the item exists to prevent — an outflow and an inflow counted that never crossed the perimeter — needs both legs inside contours, and a movement to an outside account genuinely does cross it; (2) transfer_relationships_action builds candidates from every other account with no scope filter, so the pair stays discoverable from the inside end, pinned by a new test; (3) account_scope is derived per call from contours and exclusions, never recorded, so bringing the account into a contour brings the item straight back. Nothing is permanently silenced.

Merged as afeea2e; make lint and both crates' tests green after the merge.

title: The scope action's sentence names two ways out and its target names one
description:
`account_scope_undecided` reads: «Add it to an existing contour, or record that it is outside the perimeter and why.» Its `target` is a single `ActionTarget::Operation` naming `AddContourVersion` (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:1623). The second way out — `PUT /v1/accounts/{id}/scope`, which exists and works — is reachable only by a client that reads the prose and then goes hunting through the specification.

An agent that treats `target` as the contract, which is what `target` is for, can only ever put the account inside a contour. Reported by an external reviewer, who found the endpoint and asked why the queue would not offer it.
design:
`ActionTarget::Operation` becomes one of possibly several. Either the target grows a list — `resolution_options: [{operation, request}]` — or the queue emits the alternatives beside the single `target` it keeps for compatibility.

Whichever shape wins, the invariant to state in a test is the one that was broken: for every action whose `reason` names N ways to close it, the published operations number N. That invariant is checkable only if the ways are enumerated somewhere other than the sentence, which is the argument for putting them in the type.

Same defect probably lurks wherever an action has more than one honest resolution; audit the other kinds while here.
close_reason: ActionTarget gained Options(Vec<ResolutionOption>), each option carrying its own RequestPlan, with from_options normalising so one way out keeps a single encoding and every existing action serialises byte-identically. account_scope_undecided now publishes both AddContourVersion and RecordAccountScope, the latter presetting disposition=outside and marking /reason owner-supplied. Audit of all fourteen ActionKinds filed as iaam-1lqx and iaam-08y3. Committed in 58f9add.

title: There is no way to require that a confirmation came from the owner and not from the agent
description:
Raised by the owner 2026-09-03, deciding that `AnswerClassificationQuestion`
keeps `Scope::Agent`.

His reasoning, and it settles the vocabulary: **the agent is the interface.**
Restricting its scope does not protect the owner, it disables the interface. The
agent acts on the owner's will, so a token scope is the wrong instrument for
"this decision is the owner's" — `ActionState::NeedsOwnerInput` already says
that, and `required_scope` says who may transmit the request. The two are
different questions and the model already separates them.

What is left unanswered, in his words: "конечно никто не мешает агенту выполнить
что-то произвольное. Как с этим быть не очень понятно." Nothing distinguishes a
request the owner asked for from one the agent decided on. For most acts that is
acceptable — the agent is the interface and the journal is auditable. For some
it may not be.

His suggestion: a one-time code known only to the owner, requested for the acts
where the confirmation must demonstrably be his.

Worth deciding before it is needed rather than after. The acts that plausibly
qualify are the ones whose effect outlives the request: answering a
classification question records a durable rule that settles every later row it
matches; retracting an import removes facts; confirming a transfer pairing
rewrites two events into one.

Not urgent. Filed so the question is not lost, and because the reasoning above
is worth keeping whether or not a second factor is ever added.
acceptance_criteria:
- A decision: which acts, if any, require evidence that the owner personally confirmed them, and what that evidence is.
- If a second factor is chosen: it is requested only for those acts, it cannot be replayed, and the agent cannot obtain it by asking the owner for something that looks routine.
- If no second factor is chosen: that is recorded as deliberate, with what it means for an agent acting outside the owner's intent.

title: Committing an import session is two store calls, not one
description:
Named by the worker who built the session foundation (iaam-3kru).

Commit writes the journal events and then closes the session, in two calls
against the store. A failure between them leaves the two disagreeing.

Related: iaam-ge08 records the same shape for `sync_broker` — the scenario has
never been atomic across its writes, and making it so is a store-level question
about a transaction spanning a scenario, not a fix inside either caller.
acceptance_criteria:
- Writing the session's events and closing the session either both happen or neither does.
- A failure between them leaves no session that reports itself committed while its events are absent, nor events with no session that accounts for them.

title: A declared source's account is not required to agree with the operations it carries
description:
Found by codex while reviewing the multi-bank feedback; verified in the tree.

`ingest_operations` derives the source identity from `request.source.account`
and channel, then submits `request.operations`, each carrying its own
`operation.account`. Nothing checks that they agree.

So a batch declared for account A can carry rows for account B. Those rows are
recorded against B and stamped with A's source identity, which is what
`correct_import` retracts on. A retraction of A's import then reaches into B.

Compounds iaam-p2lw, where that identity is already coarser than its
description claims.
acceptance_criteria:
- An operation whose account differs from the declared source's account is refused, or the disagreement is a deliberate, documented capability.
- A retraction keyed on the declared source cannot leave rows it should have retracted, nor take rows it should not have.
close_reason: An operation whose account differs from the declared source's is refused with the structured shape. 805f957

title: Two legs of one transfer between banks are recorded as two unrelated movements
description:
Reported by an external agent importing two banks. One transfer appeared as an
outgoing movement in one bank's export and an incoming one in the other's, with
matching amount and time. iaam recorded two independent events, `cash_out` and
`cash_in`, with nothing relating them.

For a contour spanning both banks that is wrong twice over: the money looks like
it left the perimeter and separately entered it, so a flow report counts an
external outflow and an external inflow that never happened.

Nothing in the tree does this today — no pairing, no candidate mechanism, no
relation for it. `Relation` carries `Reversal` and `Replacement` only.

The caller currently has to know in advance that two rows from two banks are one
operation, and say so by constructing a single `Transfer { to }` itself.
acceptance_criteria:
- Two rows that are one transfer can be related, either as a single movement between two accounts or as two events carrying an explicit relation.
- Candidate pairs are proposed on evidence — amount, currency, date, the source's own reference, the accounts involved — and confirmed by the owner, never matched silently.
- An unmatched leg stays visible as unmatched rather than disappearing into an external flow.
close_reason: Candidate pairs proposed with evidence, related on the owner's confirmation, never matched silently; unmatched legs reported. 33f8724

title: The epic plan has no home for the spending half of the product
description:
E0 каркас, E1 ядро учёта, E2 достоверность данных, E3 рынок и инструменты, E4 разложение результата, E5 налоги, E6 оценка решений, E7 автоматизация ввода, E8 веб-UI, E9 действия и обнаружение.

Every one of them is investment-side or infrastructure. Categories, the money-flow report, the income flag on a category group, refunds and the T-Bank CSV importer were all built and shipped without an epic of their own — they arrived through E4 and through loose beads. The only bead that names the subject at the level of a goal is a closed brainstorm, iaam-ovq0, "the flow of money — income and expenses as the first goal".

So the roadmap frames the product as investment accounting exactly as the API surface did before today. That asymmetry is why work on the spending half has no place to hang, and why nothing in the plan asks whether it is finished.
design: This is the owner's call, not an agent's: an epic is a statement about what the product is for. The question is whether the spending half is a new epic beside E1-E9, or whether the existing numbering should be read differently. Do not renumber anything without him.
acceptance_criteria: Work on categories, money flow and bank import has an epic to belong to, and the plan can be asked whether that half is finished.

title: The README describes an investment ledger; the product is personal finance management
description:
The owner stated the positioning: IAAM is personal finance management, not investment accounting. The API description and the agent document were corrected today (iaam-wyp7); README.md was not, beyond its title line, which now reads «учёт личных финансов».

Its body still describes one half. It covers the three ingest channels, reconciliation by dimension, the instrument catalogue, market data and broker sync — and says nothing about categories, the money-flow report, refunds as a first-class fact, or the bank CSV importer, all of which are built and shipped. A reader who opens the README meets the same framing that made an external agent tell the owner his spending did not belong in the system.

CLAUDE.md's language rule constrains the fix: existing Russian documents are not retranslated, but anything new goes in English. A new Russian section would break that rule and an English section inside a Russian README reads badly, so the shape of the fix is a decision, not a typing job.
acceptance_criteria: A reader of README.md learns that the system accounts for spending and income as well as investments, without opening the contract.

title: An account has no kind, so the system cannot know which negative balances are impossible
description:
An account is `{ id, title, institution }` — `AccountView` (crates/iaam-app/src/ports.rs:79), `AccountDto` and `CreateAccountRequest` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:2336, :2407). There is no kind, type or class anywhere on it.

That is why `Balances::negative_cash()` carries the comment "At stage 1 this is not an error: a negative margin balance is a liability" (crates/iaam-core/src/projection/balances.rs:125). The statement is exactly as strong as the model allows: a margin account may legitimately go negative, a savings account may not, and the system cannot tell them apart, so it cannot call any minus impossible.

Surfaced by the reported case behind iaam-upig. There the minus was an artefact of a missing opening balance rather than a real overdraft, and iaam-upig fixes that. This bead is the residue: even with opening balances asserted everywhere, an account that cannot be overdrawn going negative would still pass unremarked, because nothing records that it cannot be overdrawn.
design:
A first draft of this bead said the owner should record that an account 'cannot be overdrawn'. That is too strong and the owner corrected it: a technical overdraft on a debit card is real and ordinary. What is wanted is a **warning about a probable error**, not a constraint that refuses.

So the value the owner supplies is an expectation, not a rule: 'a negative balance here is unexpected'. A negative balance on such an account is reported as contradicting that expectation and nothing more — no refusal, no suppression, no invariant. That also keeps it consistent with the core's existing stance in `Balances::negative_cash()`: at stage 1 a negative balance is not an error.

Weigh what to add before adding a taxonomy. The value here is one expectation, not a classification of banking products, and a kind enum invites every later feature to branch on it. `InstrumentKind` is the cautionary precedent in this repository: it is allowed to be unset, and the valuation is marked incomplete rather than guessed.

Whoever supplies it is the owner. An institution's product behaviour is not knowable from a statement, and inferring which account is a margin account from a transaction pattern is exactly the class of guess this repository forbids. Optional, defaulting to 'not asserted', never inferred.

Distinguish this from iaam-sbht, which wires the §11 perimeter. That one classifies a negative span from evidence — settlement terms, credit indicators — and needs no owner input. This one is the owner's expectation about an account, and it is a hint layered over that, not a replacement for it.
acceptance_criteria: The owner can record that a negative balance on an account would be unexpected; such a balance is reported as contradicting that expectation, as a warning and never as a refusal; an account with nothing asserted behaves exactly as it does today.

title: The outflow-decomposition action denies a remedy the API offers, and conflates two cases that have different remedies
description:
`flow_diagnostics` emits `UndecomposedOutflows` through `blocked_action` (crates/iaam-app/src/actions.rs:517, :424), which forces `ActionState::Blocked` and `ActionTarget::None`. `Blocked`'s own doc comment reads "No operation in this API is available for this item" (actions.rs:69). That is false: category-rule creation is in this same API. The action's message betrays that the author knew — it says no *report* operation can provide a rule — but `Blocked` has a global meaning, and the action catalogue resolves targets by scanning the whole completed contract, not a report-local namespace (crates/iaam-server/src/action_catalog.rs:38).

Owner-only is not a reason for `Blocked`. The model already expresses exactly this situation: `NeedsOwnerInput` + `required_scope: Owner` + an operation target + fields marked `ProvidedBy::Owner`. Creating the first contour is the precedent — the agent may not draw the boundary, yet the action still names the owner-only operation and its missing inputs (actions.rs:773). Category administration is genuinely owner-only (the three handlers call `require_admin`), and the queue's job is to tell the agent what to ask the owner for, not to grant it permission.

**The part that makes this more than a state relabel.** `UndecomposedOutflows` currently aggregates two materially different cases:

1. Unmatched `CashOut` and `Refund` rows — a category rule is the remedy.
2. External `CashTransfer` rows — deliberately in `not_decomposed`, and category assignment is never consulted for a transfer at all (crates/iaam-core/src/projection/money_flow.rs:165 gates the assignment to `CashOut | Refund | Income`).

Pointing every one of these actions at rule creation would therefore be false for a transfer-only aggregate and only partly true for a mixed one.
design:
Split the diagnostic at its source rather than relabelling the state:

- Rule-remediable rows: `NeedsOwnerInput`, `required_scope: Owner`, targeting category-rule creation, with the matcher and the category marked `ProvidedBy::Owner`.
- External transfers: keep `Blocked`, with a reason that says the true thing — category rules do not apply to transfers — or decide such transfers ought to be explainable and change the projection. Do not conflate the two.

Two traps found while analysing this:

- **Do not preset the report's `from`/`to` as the rule's validity interval.** A report window is not evidence that a category's meaning began and ended there.
- **There is no defensible matcher to preset today.** The aggregate retains only account, currency, count and net amount, none of which are fields of the rule request. Proposing one would need the diagnostic to keep stable row keys or source attributes, and even then the breadth of the matcher stays the owner's judgement.

Also reconsider `ActionCategory::Informational`, whose doc says "a fact that requires no action" — that contradicts emitting an owner-remediable gap. `Recommended` if decomposition is optional quality work; `RequiredForGoal` if a fully explained money-flow report is a named goal.

Analysis cross-checked with a second model against the tree; every citation above was verified in the source.
acceptance_criteria: An agent working the queue on an account with unmatched outflow rows is told the operation the owner would use and which fields only he can supply; a transfer-only aggregate says truthfully that no rule applies to it; the action category matches whether the item requires action.
close_reason: Split at the source: not_decomposed is keyed by cause. A row no rule matched yields an owner-only NeedsOwnerInput action naming the category-rule operation with matcher and category owner-supplied and nothing preset; an external transfer keeps Blocked with the true reason, since category assignment is never consulted for a transfer. Category moved Informational to Recommended, with the worker's argument for not going to RequiredForGoal recorded in the builder.

title: Typing a body field moves its refusal out of ApiError and into the extractor
description:
Surfaced by the worker on iaam-oqhv as a regression it could not fix inside its scope, and it is the exact defect iaam-al56 exists to remove.

Before that change, `{"namespace": "cusip", ...}` on the resolve route was refused by `crates/iaam-app/src/adapters/sqlite.rs:464` as a JSON `ApiError` with `field: "namespace"` and `expected: "isin, moex_secid, ticker, figi or broker_code"`. Now serde rejects it inside the `Json<...>` extractor first, and the wire carries `422 text/plain`:

    Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: namespace: unknown
    variant `cusip`, expected one of `isin`, `moex_secid`, ...

The enumeration still reaches the client, in the schema and in that text, so nothing became unknowable — but the shape did. The general lesson is worth writing down: **making a field well-typed moves its refusal upstream into the extractor**, so every such improvement silently converts a structured refusal into an unstructured one until iaam-al56 lands.
design: Verify after iaam-al56 merges: the uniform envelope should restore ApiError for this route with no further work. Add a contract test pinning it, so the next typed field cannot regress it again silently.
acceptance_criteria: A wrong namespace is refused as application/json ApiError naming the field and the five valid codes; a contract test pins it.
close_reason: Fixed by the uniform envelope from iaam-al56: a wrong namespace now returns application/json ApiError with field=namespace and all five codes. Contract test an_invalid_namespace_is_refused_with_the_valid_ones_named tightened to assert the envelope, not just the bytes.

title: An empty market series says nothing about completeness
description:
`complete_through` rides on each row (crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/market_reference.rs). With zero rows the completeness boundary is not returned at all, so 'the rate is unknown' and 'this instance holds no data for that period' are indistinguishable. Reported against market/key-rate returning `[]`, but prices and fx have the same shape.

The skill insists on exactly this distinction — a fact may be quoted, a missing fact must be named as missing — and the response cannot express it when the array is empty.
design: Two candidates, needing a decision before implementation: (a) wrap the response as { rows, complete_through } — breaking, but the boundary becomes a property of the answer rather than of a row, which is what it is; (b) return the boundary in a response header — non-breaking, but puts a fact outside the JSON contract an agent is told to read. Recommend (a), applied to prices, fx and key-rate together so the three series keep one shape.
acceptance_criteria: A request covering a period the instance holds nothing for returns the completeness boundary; a contract test distinguishes 'no data held' from 'no value in this interval'.
close_reason: All three market series answer { rows, complete_through }; the boundary survives zero rows and is required in the schema. Contract test distinguishes 'holds the series, nothing in this interval' from 'holds nothing at all'. SKILL.md updated to match. 1854 tests pass.

title: In market/fx from and to are currencies, and dates everywhere else
description:
`MarketFxParams` (crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs:937) reads `from: CurrencyDto, to: CurrencyDto, from_date, to_date`. Every other endpoint spells the interval `from`/`to`: reports/flow, market/prices, market/key-rate, reconciliation, market/sync.

An external agent sent `from=2026-01-01` to market/fx and was told `unknown variant '2026-01-01', expected one of RUB, USD, EUR, CNY, XAU`. One parameter name means a currency in one place and a date in another; nothing in the contract warns of it, because these fields carry no descriptions either (see iaam-mj84).
design: Rename the currencies to `base`/`quote` and the dates to `from`/`to`, so the interval is spelled the same on every endpoint and the currency pair reads as a pair. Breaking for any existing caller; the API is pre-1.0 and agent-facing, and the collision is the kind of thing that is cheap to change now and expensive later.
acceptance_criteria: market/fx takes base, quote, from, to; contract test covers the new names; no endpoint uses from/to for anything but an interval.
close_reason: market/fx takes base/quote/from/to; an interval is spelled from/to on every endpoint; merged in api-market-params.

title: Market parameters carry no descriptions: board and session reach the agent as bare names
description:
`MarketPricesParams` and `MarketFxParams` (crates/iaam-server/src/routes.rs:923-948) and `MarketKeyRateParams` have no doc comments, so the contract shows `board`, `session`, `from`, `to` without meaning — unlike `MoneyFlowParams`, `BalancesParams` and `ReturnsParams`, which describe every field.

`board` is the MOEX `BOARDID`; `session` is the ISS `TRADINGSESSION` (crates/iaam-market/src/moex/parse.rs:164; the parse test pins the evening session as 3). An agent cannot guess either. This is contract work, not skill work: the skill deliberately names no route, but the contract is obliged to carry the semantics of its own fields.
acceptance_criteria: Every market query parameter has a description in the generated OpenAPI; board and session name their MOEX origin and give the values the instance actually stores.
close_reason: Every market query parameter carries a description; board and session name their MOEX origin and what this code actually proves about their values; merged in api-market-params.

title: The instrument-resolve contract names namespace/value/on and explains none of them
description:
`ResolveInstrumentRequest` (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:4275) declares `namespace: String`, `value: String`, `on: Date`. `namespace` and `value` carry no doc comment, so the generated contract shows names without meaning, and `namespace` is typed as a free string although the domain admits exactly five values — `isin`, `moex_secid`, `ticker`, `figi`, `broker_code` (`AliasNamespace`, crates/iaam-core/src/instrument.rs:82).

An external agent reported three failed attempts (`code_kind`, `code`, `as_of`) before reading the schema, and the schema still did not say which namespaces exist. The skill speaks of an 'external code' that 'resolves as of a date'; no word of that vocabulary reaches the contract.
design: Type the field as an enum in the schema so the permitted values are enumerated, and add doc comments tying each field to the skill's vocabulary: namespace+value together are the external code, on is the document's date. Compare with the report parameter structs, which already carry descriptions.
acceptance_criteria: The generated OpenAPI enumerates the five namespaces and describes all three fields; a wrong namespace is refused with the enumeration in ApiError.expected.
close_reason: The resolve request types namespace as an enum of the five registers and describes all three fields; merged in api-resolve-vocabulary.

title: A not_computable code carries no prose, so the document has to
description:
not_computable is Option<String> on four report DTOs (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:849, 989, 1017, 1123) — a bare code with no explanation. The same holds for the data_quality codes.

That is the only reason docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md still carries 54 lines mapping each code to what the agent should tell the owner. A refusal that does not say why is a refusal the reader has to look up, and looking it up is what E9 removes.

Let each refusal carry its own sentence on the wire, generated from the same enum that produces the code, so the two cannot drift. Then those sections go.
close_reason: not_computable (26 codes across five DTOs and six construction sites) and the data quality status are typed enums generated from the same macro that produces the code, and the schema publishes each code's sentence. state_newer_than_report and numeric now say on the variant that they are defect reports, not owner-facing gaps.

title: The verdict vocabulary is a String, so the contract cannot enumerate it
description:
VerdictDto.verdict is a plain String (crates/iaam-server/src/dto.rs:743). The generated OpenAPI therefore does not list the ten verdict codes, and an agent cannot learn the vocabulary from the contract.

That is the only reason docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md still carries a 46-line table explaining what each verdict means. The table is the kind of thing E9 exists to delete, and it cannot be deleted while the contract is silent.

Make the wire field a typed enum whose schema enumerates every code, and carry each code's meaning as its schema description. Then the table goes.

Note while doing it: the previous table listed eight codes of ten and omitted possible_duplicate and quarantined, both of which production emits. A generated enum cannot drift that way, which is the point.
close_reason: VerdictDto.verdict is a typed enum whose schema enumerates all ten codes, each with its meaning, generated from one macro list beside Verdict::code() so the two cannot drift. The wire is unchanged. Proved by blanking one code's meaning and watching two contract tests fail by name.

title: The balance route answers with statuses but no coverage gaps
description:
POST /v1/reconciliation/balance returns a bare Vec<ReconciliationStatusDto>, while GET /v1/reconciliation now carries a top-level gaps field (E9.T4, iaam-3y2o).

A caller that records an owner balance and reads the response back gets the taints attached to each status, but not the ledger-wide gaps — including a gap that correlates with no status, which is exactly the case T4 exists to surface.

E9.T4's spec says 'a new top-level field on the reconciliation response', singular, so this may be intended. Decide deliberately rather than by omission.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `POST /v1/reconciliation/balance` for an account and period whose ledger holds a gap that correlates with no status.
2. The response is a bare list of statuses: the gap is absent, though the reconciliation read carries it.
acceptance_criteria:
- Decided deliberately, not by omission: either `POST /v1/reconciliation/balance` carries the ledger-wide `gaps` field as `GET /v1/reconciliation` does, or the asymmetry is stated in the contract with the reason.
- If carried: a caller who records an owner balance and reads the response back sees a gap that correlates with no status — the case E9.T4 exists to surface.

title: Ingest: a refused row on the upload path writes no coverage gap
description:
EventKind::ImportCoverageGap is constructed in exactly one place, crates/iaam-app/src/scenarios/sync.rs:436 — the broker sync path. A statement upload that refuses rows produces per-row verdicts (Rejected/Quarantined) and no gap event.

Consequence: reconciliation taints nothing for an upload that refused rows, so a status can reach accepted_internal on a document whose refused rows would have moved the very dimension being confirmed. That is the failure ImportCoverageGap exists to prevent, and the upload path does not use it.

Found while designing E9.T4 (iaam-3y2o), which reports gaps but cannot invent the ones that were never written.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Upload a statement whose rows are partly refused (`Rejected` / `Quarantined`).
2. Read the journal: no `ImportCoverageGap` event was written - it is constructed only on the broker sync path.
3. Reconcile the interval: nothing is tainted, and a status can reach `accepted_internal` on a document whose refused rows would have moved the dimension being confirmed.
acceptance_criteria:
- A statement upload that refuses rows writes an `ImportCoverageGap`, as the broker sync path does.
- A status cannot reach `accepted_internal` on a document whose refused rows would have moved the dimension being confirmed.
- `EventKind::ImportCoverageGap` is constructed from both paths, so a later change to what a gap means cannot pass one of them by.

title: Error responses become RFC 9457 problem details
description:
`ApiError` (`crates/iaam-server/src/error.rs`) is a hand-rolled shape — `code`,
`message`, `field`, `expected`, `actual`, `correlation_id` — for a problem RFC
9457 standardises: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, plus
extension members, with `Content-Type: application/problem+json`.

Its §3 validation example is also the precedent we already needed: an `errors`
array of `{detail, pointer}` where `pointer` is a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) into
the request body. That is the same addressing E9's action envelope uses for
missing inputs, so adopting it makes one convention instead of two.

RFC 9457 has NO notion of remediation or a next step — the extension-member space
is empty there, and §4.2's registry is Specification Required and excludes
deployment-specific types. So E9's next-step block stays ours, carried as an
extension member, and that is the intended use of the mechanism rather than a
workaround.

## This is a breaking change to a public contract

Every error response in the API changes shape, and the media type changes with
it. It is therefore its own task, not a rider on another: doing it inside E9.T1
would change every error in the API in the same commit that introduces the entry
point.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Error responses are `application/problem+json` and carry `type`, `title`,
  `status`, and `detail` where there is something to detail.
- `type` is a URI that is stable and documented; the present `code` strings map
  to it one for one, and the mapping is written down rather than invented per
  call site.
- Field-level rejections become `errors[] {detail, pointer}` with a JSON Pointer,
  replacing the single `field` / `expected` / `actual` triple. Where `expected`
  and `actual` carry information a pointer does not, they survive as extension
  members rather than being dropped.
- `correlation_id` survives as an extension member — §15.2 requires an invariant
  violation to return an identifier and no number.
- The OpenAPI document describes the new shape, and the contract tests assert it.
- Consumers that ignore unrecognised members keep working, per §3.2.

title: One place issues a credential, not two
description:
`claim_owner` in `crates/iaam-bootstrap/src/main.rs` assembles a token record
itself — `secret_hex(32)`, `hash_token`, a fresh `TokenRecord`, `insert_token` —
because it must decide-and-create inside one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, and
`TokenAdmin::issue_token` is not transaction-aware.

That is the second implementation of credential issuance, and it is the one that
mints the OWNER token. If issuance changes — a longer secret, a different hash, an
audit record — the claim path silently keeps the old behaviour, and nothing fails.

The duplication is avoidable. `SqliteAdapter` holds `Arc<Mutex<SqliteStore>>`
(`adapters/sqlite.rs:96`), so one connection is shared under a lock: a
transaction-aware claim can live in the adapter's own blocking closure.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `TokenAdmin` gains a claim operation that decides and creates atomically, and
  the adapter implements it in one blocking closure with the transaction.
- `iaam claim` calls the port and no longer touches `iaam-store` or assembles a
  token record.
- The concurrency test keeps proving that exactly one of two racing claims wins.
- Exactly one place builds a token record.
close_reason: TokenAdmin gained an atomic claim_owner; the adapter holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE across the check and the insert in one blocking closure. MintedToken is the only place a token record is built in non-test code. The concurrency test still passes and its substance is unchanged. Verified on merged main: fmt, clippy -D warnings, and the 19-test bootstrap suite including concurrent_claims_leave_one_owner_and_refuse_the_other.

title: Token scopes reflect that the agent is the owner's surface
description:
ADR-0003. Twenty-three routes are gated by `require_admin`, and the owner has no
surface but the agent — so an agent token cannot perform onboarding at all, and
the split protects nothing, because there is no second surface to protect
against.

This is safe to change only AFTER the CLI owns token issuance and broker
credentials: what makes an owner-scope agent token acceptable is that behind it
there is no longer anything with which to seize the system.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The agent that is the owner's surface holds an owner-scope token, and the
  documentation says so plainly rather than implying an owner who calls the API.
- Every remaining `require_admin` gate is re-examined and each one either keeps
  its gate with a stated reason or loses it. The list of what stays gated is
  written down.
- `Scope::Agent` remains, with its purpose recorded: a future secondary agent
  that has no business administering.
- A test proves that an owner-scope token completes onboarding end to end, and
  that a lesser scope is refused where the gate was kept.

title: E9.T5: actions ride along where the response already holds the context
description:
The second carrier of the same envelope. A response that already holds the
context can attach the action in place, so an agent acting on a specific call
does not have to re-query the frontier.

The rule is context, not sentiment: an action rides along only where the
producing response has it bound. Report queries know the contour and interval;
broker sync knows broker, account and period; document upload knows the document
hash and inferred period; a rejected row knows its ingestion operation.

Bare `Provisional` is left WITHOUT an action until its result carries a
reconciliation target. It carries an event id and nothing else today, and there
is no event-read endpoint through which a client could recover the rest. An
action there would be invented. Whether to enrich the scenario result instead is
decided in this task, with its cost stated.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The same envelope and the same route resolver as E9.T1. Two carriers, one
  truth. It is NOT required that every verdict carry an action.
- Each attachment named with the context that makes it honest, and a test that
  the attached subject is fully bound.
- Where an action would require context the response does not hold, there is
  none, and the task records why.
close_reason: Three carriers gain an always-present actions array rendered through the one action_dto that /v1/actions uses: reconciliation, the flow report, and broker sync. The scoped ledger diagnostics are a sibling function filtering on typed gaps and statuses, computed inside the scenario that already holds the ledger so the journal is folded once. Verified independently: make check 1831 tests, and the two-items-per-duplicate rule proved by making the sync carrier drop the second item.

title: The owner speaks to an agent, and a CLI keeps the secrets (ADR-0003)
description:
The owner has no surface but the agent, so no response ever tells a human to make an HTTP call. Every call is made by the agent; what a response carries is where a missing value comes from — the owner's knowledge, an external document, or state already held.

The CLI is rewritten from environment variables into real subcommands and limited to secrets and the trust root: instance claim, token issuance and revocation, broker key generation and rotation, broker access credentials. The line is drawn at secrets, not at 'initial setup', because 'setup' has no edge and would creep until the CLI is a second application. provision.rs already keeps a broker token out of logs, errors and the database; sending it through a chat message would defeat that.

The agent therefore holds an owner-scope token. Scope::Agent stays for a future secondary agent. This is safe only because the dangerous operations left HTTP entirely: behind that token there is nothing left with which to seize the system. As it stood, the Owner/Agent split protected nothing — it presupposed a second owner surface that does not exist — and only made 23 routes unreachable for the sole client.

The order of setup is written nowhere: not the CLI, not the agent skill, not the coming web UI. It is computed from state as a queue of outstanding actions that every surface reads. Evidence for why: docs/agent-skill/SKILL.md claims four routes answer 501 whose handlers are implemented. Three hand-written wizards would drift the same way.

Accepted risk: an owner-scope agent token reads and writes everything that is not a secret. Bounded by the decision itself — it cannot mint tokens or reach broker credentials, and is revoked from the console.

title: An agent can deploy and configure this from one document
description:
The reader is an agent, not a person browsing a README. It arrives with a
checkout or an image reference, no memory of this project, and it must reach a
running, configured, reachable server without asking anybody a question it could
have answered from the text.

That premise is the same one E9 states for the API — the answers direct the
agent, so no skill has to — applied to getting the thing running at all.

## What "agent-first" has to mean here, concretely

- Every step is a command with its expected output, not prose describing an
  intention. A step whose success cannot be checked by running something is not
  a step.
- The failure of each step names the next call: what is missing, who supplies it
  (the operator or the environment), and the command that supplies it. Same
  shape as the API's own answers.
- Nothing is left to the reader's judgement without an explicit default, and
  every default is stated as a value, not as "a sensible path".
- Configuration is enumerated: what is required, what is optional, what is a
  secret, what is a run-time input that must never be baked in (the account map
  and the counterparty map, per the privacy rule).
- Verification is part of the instruction, not an afterthought: the guide ends
  with a call whose response proves the deployment works, and a first import
  that proves it holds data.

## Routes to cover

- Container image (depends on iaam-za3e).
- The binary from a checkout — `cargo build --release`, where the database
  lands, how it is created.
- Whatever third route survives scrutiny: a prebuilt binary, or a compose file
  for server plus volume. Decide during design rather than promising both.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An agent with no prior knowledge of this repository reaches a health-check
  answering 200 and a first successful import by following one document.
- Each deployment route is complete on its own: no step says "see the other
  section" for anything required.
- Every configuration key is listed with its type, whether it is required, its
  default, and whether it is a secret.
- Failure modes an agent will actually hit — port taken, database path not
  writable, token missing, migration not applied — each name the command that
  resolves them.
- The document contains no value belonging to the operator: paths and tokens are
  described by shape and supplied at run time.
close_reason: docs/deployment.md rewritten agent-first: every step is a command with the output that proves it, every failure names what is missing and the command that supplies it, every path is a literal value. Container route executed end to end against a running image; the binary and systemd route is documented but was not run, and the report says so.

title: The import tools are readable by any agent, not only Claude Code
description:
The import skills live in `.claude/skills/` with a `SKILL.md` carrying Claude
Code's frontmatter. Everything an operator actually runs is a Python script
taking explicit arguments — `import.py --account-map …`, `migrate_categories.py`
— so the mechanics are already agent-neutral. Only the packaging is not: another
agent (Codex, OpenCode, Copilot, a person with no agent at all) has no reason to
look in `.claude/`, and no entry point that tells it what these tools are.

This matters more here than in most repositories: the founding design has the
agent as an external client, so the operator may well run the import from
whatever tool he has open, and the tools must not be readable by one vendor only.

## Open questions to settle before implementing

- Where the canonical copy lives — a vendor-neutral directory (`tools/`,
  `skills/`) with `.claude/skills/` pointing at it, or the reverse.
- Whether the pointer for other agents is `AGENTS.md`, a README, or both.
- Whether duplication is refused outright: two copies of an importer drift, and
  the drift is silent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The scripts and their fixtures live in one place that names no vendor, and
  each carries usage documentation readable without Claude Code's frontmatter
  conventions.
- Claude Code still discovers them as skills, with no copy of the script or the
  fixtures — a pointer, not a duplicate.
- At least one other agent's convention is served explicitly (AGENTS.md or the
  equivalent), naming what the tools do and how they are run.
- A person with no agent can run either importer from the documentation alone.
- `make check` passes, and the privacy guard still refuses a data file outside
  the synthetic-fixture directories wherever the fixtures end up.
design:
POLICY-CHANGE JUSTIFICATION (check-diff-lint.sh).

File touched that the guard classes as quality policy:
  scripts/check-no-personal-data.sh

The change RELOCATES an existing allowance rather than widening it. ALLOWED_DATA_DIRS
listed '.claude/skills/[^/]+/fixtures/'; the fixtures moved to tools/, so the entry
becomes 'tools/[^/]+/fixtures/'. One directory shape out, one in.

It is a tightening in the direction that matters for this bead: a fixture copied
back under .claude/ is now REFUSED, which is the mechanical enforcement of 'a
pointer, not a duplicate'. Without it, nothing would stop a second copy of an
importer's fixtures from appearing and drifting silently.

The guard's own self-probe was extended to assert both halves — the newly allowed
path and the newly refused one — because a relocated allowance that is asserted
but not proven is how a guard quietly stops guarding.
close_reason: The importers live in tools/ with their fixtures and their own READMEs; .claude/skills/ holds pointers with no script and no fixture; AGENTS.md serves other agents. Duplication is refused mechanically by the privacy guard, whose self-probe now asserts both the allowed and the refused path. import.py verified from its new location against the synthetic fixtures.

title: The server ships as a container image
description:
The server is run from a checkout today: there is no Dockerfile, no compose file
and no published image. `crates/iaam-bootstrap` builds the single `iaam` binary,
which is the whole deployable.

## Open questions to settle before implementing

- Runtime shape: the binary plus a SQLite file on a mounted volume, or a
  separate data container?
- Which configuration the image reads from the environment, and which must stay
  a mounted file (the account map and counterparty map are run-time inputs by
  the privacy rule and must not be baked into an image).
- Whether the image is built for the owner's machine only, or published.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A multi-stage Dockerfile builds `iaam` from a clean checkout and runs it as a
  non-root user on a minimal runtime base.
- The image contains no data file, no key and no map: everything the privacy
  rule calls a run-time input is mounted or passed in the environment.
- The database path, bind address and any secret are configuration, not
  defaults compiled into the image.
- Documented: one command builds it, one runs it, and the health endpoint
  answers.
- `make check` still passes; the build is reproducible from the committed
  lockfile.
close_reason: Multi-stage Dockerfile, fixed non-root uid 10001, deny-by-default .dockerignore. The image carries no database, key, map, token or bind address, and no default for any of them. Verified by an actual docker build and a live run of every admin subcommand and the API surface, including that the broker plaintext is absent from the database file.

title: Report parsers ship a constant fake document hash as provenance
description:
crates/iaam-ingest/src/report/tinkoff.rs:32 and finam.rs:31 define constant
all-zero and all-one hashes, and production `locator()` (tinkoff.rs:682,
finam.rs:687) consumes them. Every row of every report therefore claims the same
document identity.

Provenance is supposed to answer "which document did this come from". A
placeholder that never varies answers it falsely, and per-document traceability —
the thing the documents store exists for — is meaningless for reports.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Parse two different T-Invest (or Finam) reports.
2. Compare the `locator()` of a row from each: both carry the same constant hash, so both claim the same document identity.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A parsed row's locator carries the hash of the document it actually came from.
- Two different reports produce different locators; the same report re-parsed
  produces the same one.
- No constant stands in for a hash on any production path.

title: The broker factory hard-rejects every broker but one, so the Finam client is unreachable
description:
crates/iaam-app/src/adapters/sqlite.rs:650 branches on `code.as_str() != "tinkoff"`.
iaam-broker ships a complete Finam client and its dictionary seed
(finam/dictionary_seed.rs) that this factory can never open.

This is the shape R8 forbids — one institution baked into a branch rather than a
registry lookup. The per-broker PARSERS are not the problem: they sit behind the
ReportParser trait and I6 of the bank-import design permits them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure broker access with any code other than `tinkoff` - Finam, for which `iaam-broker` ships a complete client and dictionary seed.
2. Opening the channel fails: the factory branches on an equality test against one name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A broker is opened by looking its code up in a registry, not by an equality
  test against one name.
- The Finam client is reachable through the same path as the T-Invest one.
- Adding a third broker requires no edit to the factory.

title: Moving or copying the database must not lose the write-ahead log
description:
Found the hard way while relocating the database to ~/.local/share/iaam.

The store runs SQLite in WAL mode, so recent writes live in <db>-wal rather than
in the main file. A plain `cp` of the main file after deleting the -wal silently
produced a database missing the most recent work — 28 categories, 40 rules and 5
events — with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The project documents how to move or back up the database safely: either
  `sqlite3 <db> ".backup <dest>"`, or a checkpoint before copying, or copying
  all three files together.
- Where the project itself copies or relocates a database, it uses that method
  rather than a bare file copy.
- A reader who has just stopped the server is told that stopping it is NOT
  enough to flush the log.

title: A refund reads as money arriving from outside, inflating income
description:
Found while reading the first real August report (iaam-p5z3).

A merchant refund is submitted as a `deposit`, so the flow report counts it under
"came in from outside" and the original purchase stays under "went out". Both
sides are overstated by the refunded amount, and the household reading of
"сколько мне пришло" becomes wrong.

In August this was 4 ₽ — four 1 ₽ card authorisation charges from one merchant,
each returned the same day — so it changed nothing. A returned appliance would
put tens of thousands into "income" that nobody earned.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A refund is distinguishable from an arrival, either as an operation kind of
  its own or by netting against the charge it reverses.
- The flow report's "came in from outside" excludes it.
- The original purchase's category decomposition reflects the net, or the report
  states that it does not.
- The owner is not asked to identify refunds by hand for the common case where
  the source shows the charge and its reversal on the same account.
close_reason: EventKind::Refund added, schema 11, skill distinguishes refunds; August came_in is now 0.00 with residual 0.00

title: csv_source::Row has no source_category, so the bank's own category is lost
description: crates/iaam-ingest/src/csv_source.rs:216. OperationDto carries source_category and the category rules depend on it (money-flow design §3: one rule per source category value is what makes automatic categorisation true on the first import). The canonical CSV cannot express it, so anything arriving through /v1/ingest/csv is undecomposable by the source-category rule and falls to description rules or to not_decomposed. Found while writing .internal/specs/2026-09-01-bank-import-skill-design.md (iaam-mksb).

- `csv_source::Row` carries the source's own category, so the canonical CSV can express what `OperationDto` already carries.
- A file imported through `/v1/ingest/csv` is decomposable by the source-category rule, not only by description rules.
- Automatic categorisation is true on the first import for a bank export that names its own categories (money-flow design §3).

title: POST /v1/ingest/csv mints a random source, so a re-import duplicates everything
description:
routes.rs:1532 calls SourceId::new_random() per request — the same defect iaam-5jhq fixed for /v1/ingest/operations (routes.rs:1416, now SourceId::declared). Consequence: importing the same file twice through the csv route creates a second copy of every row instead of matching the first. Either accept a DeclaredSourceDto here as the operations route does, or document the route as the canonical hand-edit format and not an import channel. Found while writing .internal/specs/2026-09-01-bank-import-skill-design.md (iaam-mksb).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import a file through the CSV ingest route.
2. Import the same file again.
3. Every row is duplicated: the route mints a random source per request, so the second import matches nothing from the first.
acceptance_criteria:
- Decided: either `/v1/ingest/csv` accepts a declared source as `/v1/ingest/operations` does, or the route is documented as the canonical hand-edit format and not an import channel.
- If it stays an import channel: importing the same file twice matches the first import instead of duplicating every row.
